item.title: Paramount's Path to Avoid the $7B Termination Fee
item.description: The market expects that Paramount would owe Warner Bros. Discovery $7B if it does not close their merger on account of the lawsuit brought by the State AGs & the WGA. There is a path for Paramount…
item.content:encoded:
The market expects that Paramount would owe Warner Bros. Discovery $7B if it does not close their merger on account of the lawsuit brought by the State AGs & the WGA. There is a path for Paramount to owe Warner Bros. Discovery no fee, which I will argue below. This is not a prediction; it is a scenario analysis that I don’t see covered elsewhere.

Under Which Conditions does the Termination Fee Apply?

The $7B Termination Fee applies if Paramount does not close the merger by March 4, 2027, subject to one automatic extension to June 4, 2027, on account of failing to secure regulatory approvals or the presence of a governmental order prohibiting the transaction from closing.

All Regulatory Approvals Are Secured

On August 14, 2026, Paramount issued a press release with the following statement: Paramount Skydance has satisfied all regulatory clearances required under the merger agreement to close its proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery.

With all regulatory approvals in-hand, the only outstanding item prohibiting the transaction from closing is the “No-Close Order.” It is also the only outstanding item that could trigger the termination fee as well as the automatic extension to June 4, 2027.

Is the No-Close Order an Injunction?

Paramount filed a motion yesterday arguing that their agreement not to close the merger, or the “No-Close Order,” is an “injunction” and should be classified as such by the court.

The No-Close Order is an agreement made between Paramount and the Plaintiffs (State AGs & WGA) not to close the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery by as late as June 2027, pending the outcome of a trial on the merits of the case brought by the Plaintiffs.

The reason that Paramount is arguing that the No-Close Order is an injunction is to force the Plaintiffs to post a bond to cover the damages Paramount believes they are owed should they succeed at trial. Paramount’s argument is that an antitrust law, specifically the Clayton Act, requires Plaintiffs to post bond in this scenario. Paramount believes the bond should cover expected damages, which they estimate to be at least $1.88B, the same amount as the ticking fee payment owed to Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders.

To force the Plaintiffs to post bond, Paramount needs the court to find the No-Close Order an injunction per the Clayton Act, an antitrust law. It follows that a finding that the No-Close Order is an injunction is a finding that the No-Close Order is a governmental order under antitrust law.

The judge will ultimately determine whether or not the No-Close Order is a governmental order under antitrust law.

If the judge rules the No-Close Order is not an injunction under the Clayton Act, it does not satisfy the condition of being a “governmental order as a result of any antitrust law”, and therefore does not trigger the Termination Fee Payable by PSKY to WBD.

item.title: The Ellisons Should Sell a Studio to Elon
item.description: Argument: the Ellison family should divest one of the film studios (Paramount Pictures or Warner Bros.) to Elon Musk. In three points. 1. Rob Bonta will not budge on “behavioral” remedies (e.g.…
item.content:encoded:
Argument: the Ellison family should divest one of the film studios (Paramount Pictures or Warner Bros.) to Elon Musk. In three points.

  1. Rob Bonta will not budge on “behavioral” remedies (e.g. agreements to release a certain number of films annually). He won’t move off of his position that he wants “structural” remedies (a breakup of the company) as part of any settlement.

Rob Bonta has been steadfast in his commitment that the Paramount - Warner Bros. Discovery merger is unlawful and would require structural remedies to close. He has repeated this point even after it became common knowledge that Ellison would make a commitment to release a set number of films in theaters as a behavioral remedy. If Bonta won’t accept a behavioral remedy on the film side, then the easiest path to close the deal would be a divestiture of one studio by Ellison. His appetite to do so is unclear, but there is one way it could work.

Assume Ellison has to divest a film studio to close the deal. What’s the least painful way to accomplish this? Divest to an ally.

Divesting to an ally retains business relationships between the two studios. For the sake of argument, let’s assume Ellison divests Warner Bros. Studios to Elon Musk. What does this accomplish?

  • Warner Bros. films still appear on Ellison’s streaming service, Paramount+, even though he doesn’t control the production of those films. This is easily achieved through a contractual agreement, and is something that could be worked out with an ally.
  • There is no antitrust case in selling to Elon Musk. He is an individual. He could also acquire it via SpaceX or another one of his companies. The point still stands: there is no antitrust risk in Elon Musk or a Musk-controlled company acquiring a film studio.
  • Importantly, a divestiture to Musk creates a new competitor in film that could stand on its own. Antitrust regulators care about competition, and divesting an asset just to get under a market concentration percentage is of no use if the divested assets wither and die in their new form. The divested studio will have the resources of the world’s richest man. And being one of the biggest studios in the world, it would have no problem standing on its own, freed from the Discovery Global cable networks.
  • Musk’s control of the film studio creates an opportunity for him to invent a new studio business model, one heavily reliant on AI and data centers. He could use the studio to reimagine what it means to make movies, consistent with his X.com post that he will release an AI-generated version of The Odyssey this year (see next point).
  1. Musk has a fixation with Hollywood

Hollywood is on Elon Musk’s mind, and it has been for years. He has tweeted things like “Cancel Netflix for the health of your kids”, “Cancel Netflix”, “Popcorn Emoji” in a response to Paramount’s hostile bid for Warner Bros. in Dec 2025, “Disney has a major content problem. Almost their entire upcoming slate is unwatchable. They are the world’s biggest example of go woke, go broke lol.” , and most recently “Before this year ends, Grok Imagine will make a full-length movie of The Odyssey that is historically accurate and true to the art of Homer”. Musk felt the need to buy Twitter to fix social media to his liking. He could very well do the same with Hollywood.

  1. Larry Ellison and Elon Musk are close

Musk and Ellison are close. Ellison remarked on his friendship with Musk in 2018 when he revealed a stake in Tesla: “My second-largest investment, I will disclose it now, I am not sure people know I am very close friends to Elon Musk and I am a very big investor in Tesla,” Ellison said on a call. Anyone who followed Musk’s takeover of Twitter is familiar with the text exchange between Ellison and Musk, asking Ellison to finance the deal for a billion or two dollars. Finally, it was revealed in a recent NYT article that Ellison is building a house on the island of Lanai for his good friend Musk, whom the Times described as “a regular visitor”. These two are close which makes it easier to get a deal done at all, not to mention one done quickly and at the right price.

item.title: What Versant implies about the price of legacy TV
item.description: Investment Thesis With the conclusion of the Netflix / Paramount / Warner Bros Discovery bidding war on the horizon, we are about to see a transaction comparable print for Versant. My hypothesis…
item.content:encoded:
Investment Thesis

With the conclusion of the Netflix / Paramount / Warner Bros Discovery bidding war on the horizon, we are about to see a transaction comparable print for Versant. My hypothesis is that the transaction comparable is likely to come in at 5x EV/EBITDA, well above where VSNT trades in the public market today. While I do not expect an imminent re-rating to this price, nor do I expect an imminent take-private in Versant, the transaction comparable should highlight to investors the value of Legacy TV assets. Said another way, Versant’s current price reflects a purchase price that is attractive when measured against the yardstick of value to a private owner. The stock trades at 3.1x ’25 EV/EBITDA and 3.1x ’25 FCF today and has a lightly levered balance sheet at 1.1x net leverage. This valuation margin of safety gives the investment staying power as we wait for a take-out.

Company Overview

Versant Media Group (“VSNT”) is a “house of brands” mass media company, recently spun off from Comcast, that manages a diverse portfolio of legacy cable networks including USA Network, CNBC, and MSNBC. The company also holds valuable digital assets such as a majority stake in Fandango Media, Rotten Tomatoes, and various sports technology platforms.

The Transaction Comparable

What follows is a bit of a variant perception on the Netflix / Paramount / Warner Bros Discovery bidding war. From this variant perception, we can draw a conclusion about the valuation of Legacy TV assets, of which Versant is the closest publicly traded comparable and hence the subject of this writeup. I think it is well-founded, but like any good variant perception, it will probably be vehemently disagreed with because it conflicts with what we have all read in the press despite being consistent with company filings (not press reports and trade rumors), company actions and incentives. Since this is a variant perception, I do not think it is reflected in VSNT’s price at all, and therefore poses little downside risk to the shares should it not materialize. Heads I win, tails I don’t lose (much).

Discovery Global Networks (“DG”) is Versant’s closest comparable, and is about to be sold. Warner Bros Discovery (“WBD”) signed a merger agreement with Netflix to sell their studios and streaming business, excluding DG, for $27.75 per share. Paramount bid $30 per share for the entirety of WBD, putting an implied valuation of $2.25 per share on DG. WBD rejected Paramount’s bid. Subsequently, WBD put out their own valuation of DG at $4.63-$6.86 per share. Paramount volleyed back with a verbal bid from their banker at $31 for the entire company, which implies they’re raising their bid for DG to $3.25 per share. The WBD board said they expect a higher price than that. I think a base case is that we land at $4/share for DG, or 5x EBITDA. My view is that this price is arrived at as early as Monday, February 23, when Paramount’s special waiver to negotiate with the board of WBD expires.

WBD’s Board thinks DG is worth between $4.63-$6.86 per share:

The overall low to high latest 12 months adjusted EBITDA multiples observed for the selected diversified transactions were 7.9x to 16.5x, the overall low to high latest 12 months adjusted EBITDA multiples observed for the selected U.S. linear transactions were 6.5x to 11.2x and the latest 12 months adjusted EBITDA multiples observed for the selected international linear transactions were 7.0x to 8.7x. Allen & Company and J.P. Morgan applied a selected range of latest 12 months adjusted EBITDA multiples derived from the selected transactions of 5.5x to 6.5x to the latest 12 months adjusted EBITDA (as of December 31, 2025) of Discovery Global, which indicated an approximate implied equity value reference range for Discovery Global of $4.63 to $6.86 per share.

WBD’s Board did not exercise their fiduciary out, but thinks the sum-of-the-parts is worth more than $31 per share:

We are writing to inform you that Netflix has agreed to provide WBD a waiver of certain terms of the Netflix merger agreement to permit us, through February 23, to engage with PSKY to clarify your proposal, which we understand will include a WBD per share price higher than $31. We seek your best and final proposal. To be clear, our Board has not determined that your proposal is reasonably likely to result in a transaction that is superior to the Netflix merger. We continue to recommend and remain fully committed to our transaction with Netflix and have scheduled a special meeting of our shareholders on March 20, 2026 to vote on the Netflix merger agreement.

My read of the situation is that the WBD board has not re-opened merger talks for WB streaming and studios, on account of a signed merger agreement with Netflix. The way the board would re-open the bidding is to exercise their fiduciary out, which they have explicitly not done (“To be clear, our Board has not determined that your proposal is reasonably likely to result in a transaction that is superior to the Netflix merger.”). The fiduciary out exists to allow the board to exercise their fiduciary duty to shareholders in the event a superior transaction materializes or is likely to materialize. The board explicitly said that is not what occurred with Paramount’s proposal.

Since they have not exercised their fiduciary out, you’d have to believe that Netflix re-opened the bidding process. I cannot think of any reason that a buyer would agree to re-open a bidding process after they already won. Recall, Netflix was going to withdraw their offer if WBD didn’t go exclusive and accept their terms before market open the morning following the receipt of the final bid.

To beat this point to death, look at the recent contest for Metsera to see what I mean. Metsera exercised their fiduciary out, and the buyer, Pfizer, was so upset that they sued Metsera for breach of contract, breach of fiduciary duty, and tortious interference. Which is what you’d expect a buyer to do if they were about to lose a signed deal. Metsera was right in exercising their out because it was that action that caused a bidding war. We don’t have that here in Netflix / Paramount / Warner Bros Discovery.

Since the spin-off of DG is a closing condition of the merger, it is in WBD’s and NFLX’s mutual interest to get Paramount to stop making so much noise and settle on a price for DG. And that’s what I think is happening here. I think Netflix let Paramount under the tent to finally agree upon a price for DG. Then, when the shareholder vote comes on March 20, WBD shareholders will know exactly what they are voting on, as a merger agreement for DG will remove the debt reallocation mechanism that threatens to reduce the cash consideration in the Netflix merger.

If you disagree with my variant perception, and think that we are heading into a bidding war between Netflix and Paramount for WBD, then I think that situation does not argue for a lower valuation for DG than what I have argued so far.

Valuation

In 2025, Versant did $6.6bn in Revenue, $2.2bn in Adj. EBITDA, and $1.4bn in FCF. The stock trades at a 3.1x ’25 EV/EBITDA multiple and 3.1x ’25 P/FCF multiple. The valuation is low, likely due to the company being in a hated sector (legacy TV) and being a newly formed company, as it was a spin-off that completed in early January of this year.

At 5x EBITDA, the stock has ~97% upside. It’s logical to think that Comcast would prefer to spin Versant before selling it to a strategic or private equity buyer, effectively a disguised sale.

Risks

As it stands today, this is a business whose financial profile is dominated by Linear TV. And we all know that Linear TV is in decline. In 2024, 17% of revenue was from non-pay TV (platforms, digital advertising, and other). VSNT’s 3-5 year goal is to shift this mix to ~33%, and their long-term goal is to reach ~50%. I don’t have a strong view if they are likely to achieve their stated goals given the newness of this company and limited track record. Should they not achieve their goals, absent a stabilization in linear TV, we’re looking at a melting ice cube.

Another risk to this thesis is that Brian Roberts maintains ~33% voting control in Versant through his high-vote Class B shares. Roberts has historically not been a seller, and could stand in the way of any sale. Versant also has growth aspirations in digital, and could poorly invest excess capital at the expense of shareholders. I think this risk is somewhat mitigated by the presence of David Novak as chairman of the board, the impressive former CEO of Yum! Brands. Further, when it was a part of Comcast, VSNT was the “cash cow” that funded Comcast’s buildout of Peacock. VSNT no longer serves that purpose, its cash flow is its own, and to me that suggests that Roberts might be willing to let it go.

Another risk is that Paramount and Warner Bros Discovery do not come to an agreement on the value of DG. My view is that Paramount has been making so much noise precisely because they want to force the issue of a sale before DG is allowed to spin-off. My view is that they want to reduce competition in acquiring this asset. So, if Paramount walks, then I’d expect other buyers to materialize for DG and VSNT in the future.

Another risk to this thesis lies in the assumption of the debt allocation in DG and what it implies for a transaction multiple. As it stands today, the WBD board expects to allocate $17bn in debt to DG. With this allocation of debt, their valuation of DG is $4.63-$6.86 per share, or 5.5x-6.5x LTM EBITDA. It is not given that DG’s capital structure will have $17bn in debt, as it could shift back to streaming and studios. One reason I believe that DG will retain $17bn in debt is that the Co-CEO of Netflix, Ted Sarandos, as recently as yesterday, is adamant that shareholders in the Netflix / WB merger will receive $27.75 in cash, i.e. the debt reallocation mechanism will not be triggered to reduce the Netflix merger consideration.

A final risk to this thesis is the merger consideration for DG. If it’s all-stock, the stock may ultimately trade poorly, and the 5x EBITDA transaction multiple that I’m expecting could prove to be a mirage.

Discovery Global vs. Versant

Discovery Global Versant
Net debt / NTM leverage ~$15bn / 3.9x ~$2bn / 1.3x
Revenue growth, 2022–2024 CAGR (7%) (5%)
Revenue growth, 2022–2026E CAGR (12%) (6%)
EBITDA growth, 2022–2026E CAGR (20%) (10%)
Live news and sports, % of 2024 audience 20%, before the loss of NBA rights 62%
Average U.S. audience, 2024 CNN 0.5mm MS NOW 0.8mm
Growth outside pay TV Limited ~33% of revenue within 3–5 years

Versant’s own comparison of the two businesses.

Catalyst

  • Discovery Global is sold or merged with a strategic buyer

  • Versant is sold or merged with a strategic buyer

  • Versant initiates a dividend

item.content:encoded:
Short on time? Jump to the AI-generated summary at the bottom

The data center sector is experiencing an infrastructure investment boom, one that has received so much attention that even companies in old economy sectors like glass manufacturing are lavished with praise in the press. Just recently, Corning was the subject of a flattering piece in the WSJ. The article describes how Corning leveraged their advantaged position in fiber optics to secure billions of dollars of contracts with tech giant “hyperscalers”. Here’s the article for background: Why a 175-Year-Old Glassmaker Is Suddenly an AI Superstar

My hypothesis is that the data center buildout should benefit more than just Corning. The burgeoning demand for fiber optics should spill over to other industry players as well. One of those companies is Optical Cable Corporation (”OCC”), the subject of this piece.

OCC is a specialty fiber optic and copper cable manufacturer, and my belief is that they are positioned to capture some of the downstream demand in niche and specialty applications where scale isn’t necessarily a competitive advantage. OCC’s history has been in specialty cables for military/tactical, harsh environment, enterprise, and custom solutions. Where more ruggedized solutions are required in the data center buildout (e.g. edge data centers), OCC should be able to play a role. OCC’s new partnership with Lightera suggests they’re positioning to capitalize on the datacenter buildout.

The company is small and not nearly as capable as Corning of landing massive contracts from hyperscalers. But the good news is that they don’t have to. Simply winning an additional $10-$20 million dollars in sales would do wonders for the company.

OCC first caught my attention in 2025 when billionaire investor Jeffrey Gendell started accumulating a position. Rarely do you see a billionaire investor buying a stake in a micro cap stock. He has been on my radar screen ever since his name appeared on the shareholder register of companies in deeply out of favor industries such as coal and oil & gas drilling.

A lot of people use quantitative screens and look for cheap stocks that show low price to earnings multiples. Gendell’s buy is like a qualitative screen. I don’t know much about Gendell other than that he appears to be successful, contrarian, and value-focused. If he’s buying, then it’s worth taking a closer look.

The first objective is to see if there is any hard asset value that protects the investment on the downside. Then, it’s worth exploring the “what could go right” case.

Downside Protection: Asset Value

The balance sheet shows the net worth of the company on an accounting basis. Stated book value is $16.5M which is $1.86 per share. We can refine the analysis from here.

The balance sheet includes a line item for “Redeemable restricted common stock” related to a stock-purchase agreement entered into between OCC and its partner, Lightera. The net cash impact to OCC for settling this quasi-liability is capped at $2M. For accounting purposes, the reduction in shareholders’ equity from the increase in the redeemable stock is calculated as the number of shares Lightera is entitled to (642,900) at its redemption value of $5.1M. The mechanics of the redeemable stock suggest OCC will never actually be “out” $5.1M; the money they owe to Lightera is capped at $2M. More on this later.

For this analysis, book value is understated by the overstatement in the redeemable stock by $3.1M. Adding this back to shareholders’ equity results in an adjusted book value of $2.20. We can refine this further still.

Real Estate

Accounting values don’t always correspond to market values. Adjusting the balance sheet for “hidden gems” makes sense if the company has valuable, marketable assets.

In the case of OCC, they own real estate. The real estate is marked on the books below market value.

The two valuable pieces of real estate are in Roanoke County, VA (HQ) and Asheville, NC.

Roanoke is assessed by the tax authorities at $8.8M. Home to OCC’s headquarters, this property also includes a light manufacturing facility. At 148k square feet (”SF”) it sits on 11.28 acres of land. The tax value has steadily increased over time and is a reasonable downside estimate of market value.

The average price per SF for Roanoke industrial properties is about $74 per SF, implying a market value of $11M for this property. This is a reasonable high end estimate of market value.

OCC’s warehouse in Asheville is 52k SF, sits on 7 acres, was built in 1982 and last sold for $1.1M in 2016. The Asheville property is assessed by the tax authorities at $2.7M. In the case of Asheville, its tax assessment is well below the market prices of similar assets.

Today, in the Asheville/Buncombe County Market, warehouses of 10k-131k SF are listed for $91-$200/SF. A conservative estimate based on market prices is $115/SF, near the low end of comparable properties and well below the top of the range. This would imply a value of $6M, more than double the value assessed by tax authorities.

Roanoke and Asheville together are worth between $11.5M - $17M, well above the historical book value of the Property Plant and Equipment held on the balance sheet at $6.6M. Adjusting for the above results in an additional $0.55 - $1.17 / share in asset value.

Adjusting stated book value for the redeemable stock and the real estate results in an adjusted book value of $2.75 - $3.37 / share.

The adjusted book value represents substantial asset backing that minimizes downside risk. It’s helpful to think that on a per share basis you’re buying $3 worth of assets, give or take. Most investors don’t buy stocks for asset value. They’re interested in earnings and cash flow, and would rather apply a multiple to either one of those figures.

Here’s another way to think of it. At a stock price of ~$3.37, the market is essentially valuing the core business at zero. At that price you’re buying assets and getting the business for free.

The Lightera Partnership

In July 2025, OCC and Lightera entered into a strategic collaboration. Lightera is part of Furukawa Electric group, a multi-billion dollar leader in optical communications. The goal of the collaboration is to expand sales for Lightera-OCC integrated products & solutions in the data center and enterprise sectors, expand OCC’s sales growth, and create shareholder value for OCC.

Stock Purchase Agreement

Lightera paid $2M for 642,900 shares of OCC restricted common stock, which implies a price per share of $3.11 and represents 7.24% of OCC’s outstanding shares. This makes Lightera one of OCC’s biggest shareholders and they’re invested in OCC’s success.

The restricted common stock has special features unavailable to regular common stock holders. It is structured with put/call features. Starting in July 2027, Lightera has the option to put its shares back to OCC at the higher of its purchase price of $3.11 or the 10-day trailing average price of OCC’s common stock. OCC has a call option to repurchase the shares on the same terms.

From Lightera’s perspective, they get to participate in the upside of the stock and their downside is capped. They can always get their money back if the stock is below $3.11 during the put exercise period. Where it gets more interesting is what happens if the stock rapidly appreciates above the $3.11 “strike” price. OCC is only required to pay back the $2M if Lightera requests it.

Specifically, OCC would pay $2M for however many shares it can buy at that price, based on the 10-day trailing average price of OCC’s common stock. In this example, if the shares were trading at $20/share, OCC would repurchase 100,000 shares for $2M, and Lightera would have to dispose of the remaining 542,000 shares on the open market.

Given the long and deep partnership between Lightera and OCC, I’d imagine that Lightera does not exercise their put if the shares are trading well in excess of the strike price. Instead, they can sell on the open market and leave themselves and OCC better off. This instrument really is structured like a convertible note, and I see no reason why Lightera would reclaim the cash directly from OCC in a scenario where the shares appreciate. While this ‘put’ could theoretically create a liquidity crunch if OCC is struggling in 2027, it is more likely a structural safety net for a multi-billion dollar partner that is far more interested in OCC’s operational success than a $2 million exit.

The Goal of the Partnership

OCC reported $73M in sales in fiscal 2025 and is a micro-cap stock. Their history is in selling cabling for military-grade applications, think rugged cables that won’t break in harsh environments. Lightera, by contrast, is part of a multi-billion dollar organization in Furukawa Electric group, a leader in optical communications.

Lightera is now OCC’s largest shareholder and benefits if OCC’s share price is higher than $3.11 after the expiration of their 2-year lockup period. OCC benefits if OCC’s share price is higher than $3.11 after the expiration of the 2-year lockup period, and is better off if they don’t have to repay $2M to Lightera.

By looking at statements made by OCC on recent conference calls we can better understand the objectives of the partnership.

OCC’s Statements on the Partnership and Market Opportunity

September 2025 Earnings Conference Call

Below is CEO Neil Wilkin’s first statement on the 3Q25 conference call regarding the just-announced partnership. OCC & Lightera combined will offer product portfolios to better serve the enterprise sector, the data center sector and others.

Wilkin continues to say that OCC’s products are more suited for Tier 2 and Tier 3 data centers, not hyperscale data centers. He also notes that the exciting growth in the market is coming from hyperscale data centers, the area in which OCC is not best suited to compete. He goes on to say AI and data center growth will be a positive for OCC.

Here OCC says they are not prepared to share the details of their collaboration except that its to expand product offerings and solutions, especially for the data center and enterprise sectors. And that Lightera is confident on the opportunity based on their direct equity investment in OCC.

Here’s Wilkin again saying that they are not “at the moment” offering products that are more hyperscale related.

That wraps up the conference call that occurred after the announcement of the Lightera partnership. What was management saying before announcing the Lightera partnership? That might help illuminate the gap in OCC’s portfolio prior to bringing in Lightera.

June 2025 Earnings Conference Call

On the June conference call in 2Q25, Wilkin establishes the following:

  • The hyperscale data center market is getting a lot of press and attention
  • OCC does not have products for hyperscale and hasn’t targeted that opportunity
  • OCC has sales in Tier 2 and Tier 3 data centers

It sounds similar to what he said after announcing the Lightera partnership. To me this suggests Lightera will allow OCC to further penetrate Tier 2 and Tier 3 data center at a minimum, and if Wilkin is sand-bagging, Lightera will allow OCC to penetrate some Tier 1 opportunities, either directly or indirectly.

December 2025 Earnings Conference Call

Finally, there was one additional conference call after the Lightera partnership was announced. In the most recent conference call in 4Q25, CEO Wilkin continues to reiterate that their product solutions offerings for the data center market are better suited for non-hyperscale data centers. He thinks multi-tenant data centers will provide growth opportunities, and that some of the MTDCs will experience cloud computing and AI-driven growth.

The stock was extremely weak after the December earnings call. I suspect that the market was hoping for more clarity regarding the Lightera partnership and data center opportunity. OCC played it down, a lot. And the stock unsurprisingly dropped. See the big vertical drop in the stock price in December, from the high $8s to the $4s, coincident with the earnings release.

What I Think is Going on Here

To recap, a small $40 million dollar market capitalization company announced a strategic partnership with and an investment from a multi-billion dollar market capitalization company whose products include hyperscaler (Tier 1) data center solutions in the middle of a booming nationwide data center buildout. The stock initially went much higher on the news. Management refused to give any guidance on the opportunity, and even played it down a bit, suggesting it allows OCC to penetrate the same Tier 2 and Tier 3 data centers markets they were targeting before the strategic partnership. The market sold the stock back down to levels most recently seen before the strategic partnership was announced (although not entirely).

At present I have at least two coherent speculations as to what is going on here. The first is what is referred to as a bullet-dodge stock grant, and the second is NOL preservation with the potential for a full-company buyout.

Bullet-Dodge Grant

I learned the following concept from Mike at NonGaap. He calls it the dark arts of corporate governance. His view, which I agree with, is that there are subtle, legal and ethically questionable ways corporate boards and management teams manipulate incentives to favor insiders at the expense of shareholders.

One of these techniques is called a bullet-dodge grant. With a bullet-dodge, a company delays an equity grant until after negative material news is released. Management knows bad news is coming and waits until after the subsequent share price drop to issue equity compensation (e.g. stock options, restricted stock units, etc.). That way, the “strike price” for the equity compensation is lower than it would otherwise be. If the board targets a dollar value for compensation, and most do, then the result is that insiders gain more shares than they otherwise would.

Now, I’m not Mike at NonGaap, I don’t know him or talk to him, and he might quibble with what I’m about to say. I suspect the following grant by OCC is a bullet-dodge. Mike might actually have a different term for this variation, but the net effect is the same.

OCC’s Proxy contains the key piece of information:

Share-based compensation to executives is issued in accordance with the Optical Cable Corporation Amended and Restated Policy for the Timing of Equity Compensation Grants Under Stock Incentive Plans, adopted by the Compensation Committee and approved by the Board on March 29, 2016. Generally, the Timing Policy anticipates annual long-term incentive equity grants for executives (and other employees) to occur on or about the first business day after January 15 of each year.

Since 2016, it is accepted and known by company insiders that stock grants are issued in January.

Continuing with the proxy:

In accordance with the Optical Cable Corporation Amended and Restated Policy for the Timing of Equity Compensation Grants Under Stock Incentive Plans, the actual number of Common Shares issued to an executive (and other employees) is generally calculated by using the average closing price per share during the 20 trading dates immediately preceding the first business day after January 15, divided by the dollar value of the share-based compensation to be received.

The price is a weighted average of the trailing 20 trading dates immediately preceding the first business day after January 15.

All else equal, management would prefer a low stock price heading into grant season. And that’s exactly what they got after the beating the stock price took after the December 16 earnings call. Management had zero incentive to talk up the stock on the December call. It would go against their own self-interest. A quick and sharp drop in the share price heading into the grant date happens to look a lot like a bullet-dodge.

What strengthens this theory is that the “bad news” from December—that OCC is targeting Tier 2 and Tier 3 data centers rather than hyperscalers—was actually stale news. Management had already disclosed this strategy back in June. If the fundamental story hadn’t changed between the July surge and the December crash, but the sentiment shifted drastically based on management’s tone, it reinforces the idea that the price drop was artificial rather than a rational repricing of growth expectations.

If we did just see a bullet-dodge then it means that the stock market’s reaction to the July partnership announcement was the right one, i.e. the best days are ahead of the company as they capitalize on the data center opportunity.

NOL Preservation, and a Potential Buyout if the Partnership Goes Well

I’d consider what follows even more speculative than what I just wrote about the bullet-dodge. But it is consistent with the scenario I see unfolding.

OCC is sitting on a LOT of net operating losses (”NOLs”), which allow the company to shield future profits from federal-level taxation. The company has $672,000 of gross NOLs under Section 382 limitations, and an addition $13 million of federal NOLs and $2.6 million of state NOLs.

For NOLs to be preserved, specific rules must be adhered to, which I won’t cover here. One way for a company to lose their NOLs is to engage in a change of control transaction.

My speculation is that OCC and Lightera might first want to utilize some NOLs while they’re working out their partnership before a potential buyout of OCC by Lightera.

Consider the following points:

  1. The partnership calls for OCC to sell Lightera products. Lightera will use OCC as a channel to increase OCC’s revenue. OCC has not been profitable for years and only in 3Q25 did their operating margin cross into positive territory at 3.1%. If the revenue from the Lightera partnership is sufficient to keep OCC profitable, then OCC benefits from shielding those profits from corporate-level taxation. In turn, Lightera gets to participate in any upside from their stock investment.

  2. OCC has an NOL Rights Plan. Think of an NOL Rights Plan as a poison pill to prevent anyone from gaining a large percentage ownership in the company, one that would complicate the preservation of the NOLs. It suggests that management would prefer to utilize the NOLs instead of having a corporate raider or strategic acquirer go hostile on the company. The path to any acquisition of OCC goes through the management and board, and the Lightera plan to first utilize some of the NOLs is a good compromise that the board could get behind.

  3. CEO Wilkin is 61 years old. He has been a Director of the company since 2001. He was promoted to CEO from CFO after a margin call crisis befell OCC founder CEO Robert Kopstein in late 2001. Wilkin took over the reigns after a spectacular collapse in the stock price.

Today, Wilkin owns 13% of the company. The other board members are 73, 79, 76 and 65 years old. This is not a young group. All Directors and executive officers as a group own 23.8% of the company. If Wilkin could see an exit at $10 or above, he stands to make >$10 million from his 1.1 million shares. A sufficiently high share price in a buyout might be enough to get Wilkin to walk away from his $495,000 annual salary (before share based awards and other compensation).

Model

For illustrative purposes I’ve included a model. I would not anchor to it. The most important points to takeaway from the model are that FY25 revenue grew 9%, gross margin expanded to 30.9%, and operating and net losses narrowed to almost breakeven (with a positive operating margin of 3.1% in 3Q25 on +22.8% y/y revenue growth and 31.7% gross margins). Not shown is the backlog which grew from $5.7M in Oct 24 to $7.3M in Oct 25.

For estimates, I assume incremental sales from four categories (and no deterioration in the run-rate business):

  1. Product Resale which is Lightera products sold via OCC channels at 17.5% distribution margins

  2. Integrated Solutions which are Bundled OCC cable and Lightera fiber solutions at 37.5% value-added margins

  3. New customers wins in data center at 30% margins

  4. Existing customer upsell at 33.5% margins

The incremental revenue contribution results in ~18% revenue growth for the next two years. This would put OCC solidly in positive profit margin territory and sales would hit about $100 million, well within their current capacity footprint, since they claim to be operating at half capacity with $73 million of sales.

I included the model to help create a framework to understand what’s possible if the company starts executing on what they suggest is an exciting opportunity.

Another small-cap electronic equipment company, RF Industries (”RFIL”), recently saw their profitability inflect from negative to positive. That’s the kind of scenario I hope to see occur with OCC. RFIL achieved slight breakeven in the last quarter of 2024, and has steadily increased to a 4% operating margin. This is similar to what my model shows for OCC. The market rewarded RFIL with a 1.7x NTM EV/Revenue multiple. RFIL has historically traded at a premium to OCC. Even if OCC achieved a 1.0x EV/Revenue multiple, on today’s sales of $73M, that’s 42% upside. If they hit $100M in sales, that’s >100% upside. If the EV/Sales multiple expands, like RFIL, the upside is even more significant. The goal isn’t to nail a point estimate for the upside; rather it’s to show that there is a positive skew if OCC delivers on their Lightera partnership.

AI Summary

While giants like Corning capture headlines with massive hyperscaler contracts, I expect the current AI-driven infrastructure boom to spill over into more specialized companies. Optical Cable Corporation—a micro-cap manufacturer of high-performance fiber optic and copper cabling—is uniquely positioned to capture demand in Tier 2 and Tier 3 data centers, as well as niche “harsh environment” applications (military, industrial, and broadcast) where specialized, ruggedized solutions are required.

Key Points

  • Asset-Backed Downside Protection: The stock trades near its liquidation value. Adjusted for “hidden gems”—specifically real estate in Roanoke, VA, and Asheville, NC—the adjusted book value sits between $2.75 and $3.37 per share.
  • The Lightera Strategic Partnership: In July 2025, OCC partnered with Lightera (part of the multi-billion dollar Furukawa Electric Group). Lightera invested $2M for a 7.24% stake at $3.11/share. This partnership allows OCC to integrate Lightera’s high-end optical solutions into its own portfolio, providing a clear path to penetrate the data center market more deeply.
  • Qualitative “Smart Money” Signal: The accumulation of a position by billionaire contrarian investor Jeffrey Gendell suggests a deep-value opportunity that quantitative screens might miss.

Catalysts

  • The “Bullet-Dodge” Theory: Recent stock price volatility following the December earnings call may have been a “bullet-dodge” event. Management had a clear incentive to let the stock price dip ahead of January’s annual equity grant cycle to secure a lower strike price for insiders, suggesting they remain bullish on the long-term outlook despite cautious public commentary.
  • NOL Preservation & Potential Buyout: OCC holds significant Net Operating Losses (NOLs) which shield future profits from taxes. Management’s use of an NOL Rights Plan suggests a desire to utilize these tax shields before any potential change in control. Given the aging board of directors and the strategic alignment with Lightera, a future buyout remains a plausible exit strategy.

Financial Outlook

Incremental sales from the Lightera partnership and data center upsells could push annual revenue toward $100 million. If OCC achieves a modest valuation multiple similar to peers like RF Industries, there is a positive skew with potential upside exceeding 100% from current levels, while the real estate assets provide a firm “floor” for the investment.

item.title: What Happens Next in Paramount’s Pursuit of Warner Bros Discovery
item.description: “Powerful writing should take one side and stick to it tenaciously, ignoring the other even though it may have merit. Objective writing is impotent.” - Dee Hock, Autobiography of a Restless Mind…
item.content:encoded:
“Powerful writing should take one side and stick to it tenaciously, ignoring the other even though it may have merit. Objective writing is impotent.” - Dee Hock, Autobiography of a Restless Mind

I’m going to make a case for what comes next in Paramount’s pursuit of Warner Bros. Discovery. The future is unknowable, and this post is highly speculative and reflects my opinion. I won’t cover every angle and instead will follow Hock’s advice to take one side and stick to it.

Paramount’s Unsolicited Tender Offer Starts the Conversation

A tender offer starts the conversation. In the case of Paramount and Warner Bros Discovery (”WBD”), Paramount’s unsolicited tender offer put WBD in-play. By ratcheting up the pressure with a series of rapid-fire, all-cash bids, the WBD board was forced to put the company up for sale, triggering its Revlon duties1.

WBD subsequently signed a merger agreement with Netflix for its Streaming & Studios business (”WB S&S”), but not for the entire company. Paramount insists that it still wants to buy the entire company, and is looking to unseat Netflix, causing them to abandon the merger agreement.

But that’s not how this has to unfold.

In fact, Paramount’s efforts to date look an awful lot like the Charter / Time Warner Cable / Comcast saga.

What John Malone’s Hostile Bid for Time Warner Cable Can Tell Us

In 2013, Charter, controlled by Liberty Media’s John Malone, launched a series of unsolicited bids for Time Warner Cable (“TWC”). At each turn, TWC found the bids by Charter to be insufficient, claiming that the price was too low, the component that included stock was too risky, and the resulting entity was too highly leveraged.

All of Charter’s bids were rebuffed. The TWC board sought a white knight, and invited Comcast to bid on the company. Comcast accepted the invitation, negotiated terms, and signed a merger agreement with TWC.

Re-read the example above and substitute Charter for Paramount, TWC for WBD, and Comcast for Netflix. The scenario is almost identical. And both scenarios, past and present, feature the guiding hand of John Malone, who is now Chair Emeritus at WBD.

What Came Next After the Merger Agreement Was Signed

What came next after TWC and Comcast signed their merger agreement is most instructive for what comes next with Paramount / WBD. Recall, Charter had launched a series of hostile bids for TWC. TWC raced to sign a friendly deal with Comcast. It’s easy to think that Charter would have continued in their dogged pursuit of TWC by raising their bid and igniting a bidding war. But that’s not what happened.

Instead, Charter signed an agreement with Comcast aimed at easing regulatory concerns around the TWC deal. Comcast created a new SpinCo to be jointly owned by Comcast / Charter 67% / 33%, Comcast sold 1.4 million existing TWC customers to Charter for cash, and Charter and Comcast swapped 1.6 million TWC customers for 1.6 million Charter customers in a like-kind exchange.

Charter put TWC in-play, TWC had to find a friendly suitor, found one in Comcast, and Charter ended up with assets in a tax-efficient manner.

The Comcast / TWC deal subsequently collapsed over regulatory concerns. And shortly thereafter, Charter signed its own merger agreement directly with TWC. Charter ultimately got their prize.

The Parallel to Paramount / WBD

The parallel to Paramount / WBD is obvious: Paramount’s hostile bids put WBD in-play. WBD sought a white knight in Netflix. WBD will dispose of certain assets.

Where the parallel breaks down, slightly, is that WBD already announced a divestiture of a business that Netflix does not want to acquire. Unlike the Comcast / TWC example, the divestiture is unrelated to easing antitrust concerns; it’s simply a disposal of an unwanted business.

Paramount can pick up the unwanted SpinCo (Discovery Global Networks, “DG”) and merge it with their cable networks business in a Reverse Morris Trust (”RMT”) transaction. More on this later.

It’s the sequencing of the disposal of the unwanted assets that is different between the two cases, and it does matter. In the case of Comcast / TWC, the disposal came after the merger agreement was signed, and the interloper (Charter) negotiated directly with the winning party (Comcast), not the company disposing of the assets (TWC).

There’s a method to this madness. The IRS does not want companies engaging in sales disguised as tax-free disposals. Had TWC simply sold assets directly to Charter for cash, the IRS would tax that as a capital gain. No good. Charter first needed to force the issue by dislodging the sought-after assets under the guise of a regulatory-driven disposal.

How does this apply to Paramount and WBD?

Instead of being a divestiture for regulatory reasons, the DG divestiture is a closing condition of the merger between Netflix and WB S&S. It rhymes with the TWC deal. The disposal of the assets is not because Paramount wants to buy them (which would constitute a plan in the eyes of the IRS). The disposal is a closing condition of a completely unrelated deal between WBD and Netflix.

WBD will separate DG in a contingent taxable / tax-free separation, depending on whether the Netflix merger closes. DG is being spun-off (”The Distribution”) in connection with the Netflix / WB S&S merger (”The Merger”). The Merger is expected to close after the Distribution. The Merger might not close at all. If The Distribution occurs and The Merger does not close, then the distribution is tax-free. To repeat, the DG spin-off is tax-free if the Netflix deal falls through. This allows DG to pursue a Reverse Morris Trust style transaction with Paramount.

The DG spin-off closing condition has been memorialized in multiple SEC documents at this point, including the merger proxy filed on January 20, 2026. Paramount has had no substantial talks with the WBD board throughout this entire process, as demonstrated in multiple press reports. The spin-off of DG is happening, not because Paramount wants it, but because it must happen in the Netflix deal. Paramount and the WBD board have never talked about the specific projections of the DG asset and have had no discussions about what it might be worth. The requirements are met for WBD to pursue an RMT of DG with Paramount.

Importantly, WBD revealed their projections and projected valuation for DG. In short, the board thinks DG is worth $4.63 to $6.86 per share in a transaction like a merger or acquisition. This is the target Paramount needs to hit if they want to pursue an RMT with DG. And they never needed to talk to the board to figure this out

Now that the merger proxy has been filed, the door is open for Paramount to drop their hostile pursuit of the entirety of WBD and focus on an RMT with DG. Just like Charter dropped their hostile pursuit of TWC and focused on picking up divested assets from Comcast / TWC.

Paramount can pick up the SpinCo (Discovery Global Networks, “DG”) and merge it with their cable networks business in a Reverse Morris Trust (RMT) transaction

For Paramount to pursue an RMT with DG, it will also need to have assets that qualify for a tax-free separation. Fortunately, they do, and the assets are their cable networks.

The cable networks, housed in the TV Media segment, are better separated from the company. The cable TV business faces different headwinds than the broadcast TV business, the streaming business, and the filmed entertainment business. Paramount shares the same rationale as WBD in wanting to separate their cable networks from their more valuable assets.

The problem with separating the cable networks into a standalone company is that they are likely too weak to stand on their own. In fact, that was one of Shari Redstone’s justifications for re-merging Viacom and CBS in 2019. CBS, the broadcast network, was far stronger than Viacom, the cable networks; Viacom found a lifeboat in CBS.

The cable networks need assistance to float, and that assistance comes in the form of a merger with DG. But first, are there any impediments to a tax-free separation of the cable networks? Below are some clues that show there aren’t any impediments and the team at Paramount has already been planning for this eventuality.

Clue #1: TV Media Preserved Continuity During the Paramount Global / Skydance Merger

The structure of the merger between Paramount Global and Skydance was done to preserve TV Media’s continuity as an active trade or business, a requirement for tax-free separations such as spin-offs and Reverse Morris Trusts.

Here’s how it worked: when Paramount Global and Skydance merged, they did not initially merge the two businesses directly. Instead, both Paramount Global and Skydance became wholly-owned subsidiaries of a New Paramount, which I’ll refer to as the “TopCo”. As subsidiaries of TopCo, the assets of each respective business were not merged into or out of any entity.

After the subsidiary transaction with TopCo, the assets of Skydance were specifically merged into the Filmed Entertainment segment of Paramount Global, leaving the TV Media segment unchanged.

Since the TV Media segment was never merged into or out of any entity, it has remained operationally and legally continuous throughout the Paramount Global / Skydance merger; only the corporate wrapper changed. With the same assets, operations, and corporate form, TV Media will pass the active trade of business test, allowing its cable network components to be spun/spun-merged tax-free.

Clue #2: Paramount’s Silence on Discovery Global Valuation is a Key Ingredient for a Tax-Free RMT

Paramount has not engaged with the Warner Bros Board in any substantive discussions regarding the valuation of Discovery Global Networks.

Paramount’s silence on Discovery Global’s valuation is a key ingredient for a tax-free RMT. Tax-free RMTs require the relevant parties to follow specific IRS guidelines to qualify for tax-free treatment. The relevant guideline here is that the parties didn’t engage in price talks about the DG asset prior to its required spin-off in conjunction with the Netflix / WB S&S merger.

We discussed this above already, but I wanted to reiterate that it is a clue that shows us Paramount’s intentions. Paramount have made it abundantly clear, in no uncertain terms, that the WBD board would not engage with them. All media portrayals of this situation suggest the parties are highly antagonistic towards one-another. In fact, the board did not even contemplate the DG projections until one day before filing the merger proxy on January 20, 2026, well after any high-level negotiations with Paramount. It’s impossible to suggest that the two parties directly discussed DG.

Now What?

Paramount is unlikely to escalate the bidding war with Netflix for WBD. Instead, they will negotiate a RMT with DG. If the TWC precedent is followed, this deal will be signed in approximately one month.

How closely this deal follows the TWC precedent is less clear to me. If history rhymes, then the Netflix deal is abandoned on antitrust grounds. Abandoning the Netflix deal would preserve the tax-free nature of the DG spin-off, which might give us a clue to the WBD board’s thinking.

As well, the WBD executives might be happier to continue to run WB S&S as a standalone company without the cable network albatross in DG hanging around their necks, especially after receiving a hefty $5.8 billion reverse termination fee from Netflix. After a sufficient waiting period for tax purposes, Paramount could yet again pursue WB S&S, just like Charter and TWC.

Another iteration: HBO Max is divested to satisfy the concerns of the regulators. Recall that Charter / Comcast negotiated a divestiture package in an attempt to clear the deal with regulators. So that could be another way this goes: Paramount ends up negotiating with Netflix for the acquisition of a specific asset with high regulatory importance such as HBO Max.

One Final Point on Paramount

Like WBD, Paramount is a collection of valuable studios & streaming assets, bogged down by cable networks. As well, Paramount houses a valuable broadcast network, a key ingredient for sports such as the NFL. You can read more about Paramount here.

WBD’s assets always had immense value, but no suitors wanted to touch the company until there was a plan to remove the bad assets. And the removal was no trivial task given the deteriorating nature of the bad assets, especially as they’re encumbered with debt.

Paramount’s fortunes could follow a similar path once the bad assets are removed from the good. There are various companies, such as Amazon, Apple, Walmart and Comcast, who should have an interest in Paramount’s studios, IP, streaming service and marquee sports rights. As mentioned above, a combination with Warner Bros. could occur down the road. A more speculative idea is that Paramount is combined with TikTok US, also controlled by Larry Ellison, in a reverse IPO after the cable networks are removed, which is a subject for another day.

  1. The board’s obligation to maximize shareholder value once a sale becomes inevitable.↩︎

New Developments

Today, January 5, 2026, marks the first full day of regular-way trading in Versant (”VSNT”). Versant is a collection of cable television properties, and some digital properties, that spun out of Comcast. Cable TV is an especially unpopular industry at the moment. By spinning off Versant, Comcast hopes that their remaining businesses will be valued more highly by the stock market. And Versant, a declining but profitable business, can refocus their cash towards their own initiatives instead of diverting it to the growth of Comcast’s other segments like Peacock (streaming).

Why should we care about Versant? Because it’s the best publicly traded comparable to what will be Discovery Global Networks “DGN” (see Part 1 if you’re unfamiliar with DGN). The valuation of DGN matters in determining the overall value of the Netflix merger. Netflix’s mixed consideration–comprising cash, NFLX shares, and DGN equity–will only be deemed superior if its combined value is greater than that of Paramount’s $30 all cash bid. The time value of money matters here as well, which will be considered separately.

At pixel time, VSNT is trading at a price per share of $40 which implies an enterprise value of $8.1B. Versant forecasts ‘26E EBITDA of $1.9B, which is a decrease of 10% from ‘25E EBITDA. Important for our read-through of DGN is the ‘27E EBITDA forecast, which is not provided by VSNT in their investor materials; I assume a further decrease of 10% in 2027.

DGN is expected to spin out of WBD in 3Q26. This means the relevant forecast period for DGN is the 12 months ending 3Q27. VSNT is trading at a 4.6x EV/EBITDA multiple for this time period, based on my estimates.

Applying a 4.6x multiple results in an implied value per share of $1.11 at the midpoint for DGN. Sensitizing it +/- 0.25x results in a low estimate of $0.72 and a high estimate of $1.50.

Above I mentioned the time value of money. In Paramount’s investor materials, they suggest a 6 month delay in closing equates to a decrease in value of $1.25 / share. They expect the Paramount deal will close at least that much sooner than the Netflix deal. You are welcome to quibble with their analysis.

All told, the Paramount deal is superior to the Netflix deal, based on my analysis. The WBD board has not provided their analysis (yet), and at this stage I struggle to see why they raced to sign with Netflix.

It wouldn’t surprise me if Paramount’s analysis is similar. It is possible that they think time is on their side, and by waiting, NFLX stock and VSNT stock will only trade down, further increasing the relative superiority of their $30 all cash bid.

At the very least, this analysis supports my earlier view that Paramount is in no rush to increase their bid.

According to David Faber of CNBC, we should hear back from the WBD board this week regarding their assessment of Paramount’s latest proposal.

Will today’s latest data point: the market value of DGN’s closest comparable, VSNT, be enough to sway the WBD board towards Paramount?

item.content:encoded:
Overview

Warner Bros. Discovery (”WBD”) entered a merger agreement with Netflix (”NFLX”) on December 4, 2025. The deal is a mix of cash and collared stock, equating to $27.75 for the streaming and studios business only (”WB S&S”) of WBD. The linear television company, Discovery Global Networks, is not included in the transaction.

Discovery Global Networks, or “DGN” will spin-out as a separate publicly traded company in 3Q 2026. A certain amount of debt is allocated to DGN from WB S&S.

If the DGN business deteriorates more than expected between now and the spin-off date, debt will be allocated to WB S&S (the company NFLX is buying) from DGN. Each dollar that is allocated to WB S&S reduces NFLX’s purchases price on a dollar for dollar basis, leaving today’s WBD shareholders exposed to a declining DGN business.

Concurrently with the exclusive negotiations that culminated in a merger agreement between Netflix and WBD, Paramount Skydance (”PSKY”) made a proposal to acquire the entirety of WBD for $30/share in cash. This bid was either rebuffed or not even considered, depending on whose story you believe.

Subsequently the board of WBD made it public that the PSKY bid was not superior to that of NFLX’s on a risk-adjusted basis. The board claimed that it required a personal guarantee from Larry Ellison, the controller and largest investor in PSKY, in order to consider the PSKY $30/share bid. Ellison delivered on the personal guarantee on December 22, 2025.

Leaks to the press since the personal guarantee suggest the WBD board still finds the PSKY bid inferior, and wants a higher price. Leaks, ostensibly from the PSKY side, suggest PSKY will not be raising their $30/sh bid. That brings us to today.

The events leading to today suggest an asymmetric risk/reward in shorting WBD if you believe the following:

  1. Sentiment Shift: Incessant press coverage has made what was once a completely ignored and unloved stock the subject of much speculation. Prominent security analysts and blog writers – those who had no interest in the stock when it was deeply discounted – are now positioned for a bidding war between PSKY and NFLX.

    • My contention is this sentiment is reflected in the WBD stock price.

    • If a bidding war were not to materialize then the shares would drop.

    Please see the (paid) link immediately below for an example of a prominent blog writer who became interested in WBD after it signed a merger agreement with NFLX, not before. He is one example of an investor positioned for a bidding war.

  1. Capped Upside: The upside in the stock is capped at around these prices if we do not enter a bidding war. The downside is tremendous in the case of a broken deal on account of:

    • a) Where WBD was trading before the merger announcement.

    • b) Hollywood studios are valued highly in control transactions, but absent that, trade poorly in the public markets (WBD’s recent history should make that point abundantly clear).

  2. The “Bid” Reality: There have been several press leaks over the last month that suggest PSKY is unwilling to move above their $30 price. There have been several press leaks over the last month that suggest WBD is unwilling to accept PSKY’s $30 bid.

    • Once it becomes clear that PSKY is not increasing their bid, the “bidding war premium” will evaporate from the share price.

    • This could bring the shares back down closer to the mid-20s which is where WBD traded after the NFLX merger announcement but before press leaks indicated that PSKY was not going away so easily.

  3. The Merger Arb / Antitrust Angle: What you’re really playing for if you’re short: WBD rejects PSKY’s $30 bid, PSKY thereafter announces that they’re withdrawing their bid. At that point, WBD’s stock price is determined by the likelihood that it can consummate the NFLX merger.

    My view is that the deal is unlikely to close as written if the government defines the relevant market as subscription streaming services.

    • The overlap between NFLX and HBO Max – combining the number 1 and the number 4 streaming services – would be an insurmountable hurdle for this deal.

    • The deal could go to court, which could cause an extended timeline to close (the drop dead date for the deal is in September 2027). Note, the timeline to close affects the trading price of WBD (i.e. the more time to close, the higher the spread, all else equal).

    • Again this has the effect of capping the risk to the short position and gives optionality for a break, upon which would send the shares sharply lower.

    The Regulatory Arguments:
    By PSKY’s estimates, Netflix would achieve a 43% share of global Subscription Video on Demand subscribers by acquiring WBD. This would result in higher streaming prices for consumers. As well, there is a monopsony argument to be made here:

    • WBD is a massive content supplier to other streamers; removing them from the marketplace would result in lower prices paid to the creative community for their work.
    • This line of argumentation was used successfully by the government in blocking the Penguin Random House / Simon & Schuster merger.

  4. The Variable Purchase Price: The deal structure implies a variable purchase price that is inversely correlated with the performance of the legacy linear business. The “Discovery Global Networks” (DGN) spin-off involves a complex debt allocation.

    • If DGN’s financial health deteriorates between now and the spin-off (3Q 2026), additional debt shifts from DGN to the entity Netflix is acquiring (WB S&S).

    • Shifting the debt reduces the purchase price received by today’s WBD investors, dollar-for-dollar.

    • Given the secular headwinds facing linear TV, this creates a tangible risk of the deal consideration shrinking below the headline $27.75 figure even if the deal closes.

    As well, the NFLX stock consideration involves a collar, and the NFLX stock price has already fallen below the floor of the collar. Using prices as of the last close, the Netflix stock consideration is ~30 cents below the headline deal price.

Where do the Shares Trade if the Deal Breaks?

WBD was trading at about $12 before the news broke that the Ellison family placed a hostile bid for the company (see image below). The shares closed Friday at $28.51 and, in my view, discount some probability of a bidding war taking place.

If the bidding war fails to materialize AND the Netflix deal ultimately breaks, there is a lot of daylight between the current price and where the shares are likely to stabilize.

Risks to the Short

Should the press leaks prove incorrect and the WBD board accepts PSKY’s bid of $30/share, I don’t see much risk to the short position, absent Netflix returning with a higher bid. Which leads me to my next point.

The biggest risk to a short position is that a bidding war does break out. Doubly bad would be a new entrant (think: big tech company) entering the bidding war, but I find that extremely unlikely.

Note: press leaks indicate WBD would walk away from Netflix if Ellison were to pay $34/share, or +$5.50 from last close.
