Seaborne thermal coal demand is expected to remain steady in the mid-900 million tonne/year range through 2030, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence and IHS Markit, driven by Indian and Southeast Asian demand. Other forecasters such as Liberum think demand will grow over this time period.

CEIX’s ability to produce coal cheaply is driven by its asset base. Its coal reserves are large and productive. The company’s mines are underground and utilize the longwall mining technique which keeps operational costs down. Lastly, the company owns an export terminal that is connected to two Class I railroads, providing it cheap and easy access to seaborne markets. The export terminal, CONSOL Marine Terminal, is located in Baltimore, MD and can export 15.0 million short tons (“tons”) per year and has a storage yard with 1.1 million tons of capacity. (One metric ton is referred to as a “tonne” and is equivalent to 1.10231 US short tons or “tons”.). It is the only east coast export terminal served by two railroads.

CEIX’s coal is high-quality: its thermal coal’s heat content is 13,000 BTU/lb which compares favorably to other U.S. coal basins such as the Illinois Basin (11,300 BTU/lb) and Other Northern Appalachian Producers (12,300 BTU/lb). As well, its sulfur content is lower, at 2.41% vs. 2.90% and 3.34%, respectively.

The company has had success leveraging its export terminal to effectively market its coal. In 2020, no individual country outside of the United States was attributed greater than 10% of total revenue, whereas both India and Europe were >10% customers in 2022. The company has been marketing more coal to the export market at an opportune time. Historically, coal export revenue tended to be derived from spot or short-term contracts with pricing determined closer to the time of shipment or based on a market index. However, the Company has recently begun to secure several long-term export contracts with varying pricing arrangements. Some domestic and export contracts span multiple years. This provides the company with more visibility than historically was the case, and at the least, paints a picture of a bright near-term future.

How does the company make money? CEIX’s mines coal at a cash cost of $28/ton and $35/ton and sold it at a price of $46/ton and $70/ton in the years 2021 and 2022, respectively. Management’s 2023 guidance calls for flat cash costs at $35/ton and a growth in realized coal revenue per ton at $81/ton. The rolling off of hedges provides a bump in revenue/ton for the company in 2023.

What’s It Worth? Valuation

There are a few ways to look at the valuation of CEIX. The simplest is to take a DCF of its thermal coal business. We know reserves, so we know how long to run the DCF which avoids complications that result from guessing the “terminal multiple” in a DCF for a non-reserve based company. The DCF is meant to be conservative and ignores any upside from the newly commissioned metallurgical coal mine, Itmann, and ignores any cash flow contribution from the export terminal.

The PAMC complex has 622 million tons of reserves. Annual production is 26 million tons, so the reserve life is 24 years. This assumes CEIX will never book another reserve, which is unlikely and therefore conservative. The real question is pricing: what’s the right price to plug into the DCF? The model is sensitive to pricing assumptions. Here’s my base case. CEIX has good visibility into 2023 and 2024 tons and pricing. I give CEIX full credit for 2023 guidance: 26 million tons at $79/ton vs. cash costs of $35/ton. What about 2024 and beyond? Since over half of 2024 tons are sold, let’s instead start with the long-term coal price. The 10Y average Central App thermal coal price is $54. Before increasing exports, CEIX has historically received 88% of that price, or $48/ton. Let’s assume in the long-term, CEIX sells 10 million tons per year at this price. This would imply 16 million tons are exported, which is 80% utilization of the export terminal. What about the export price? The 10Y average price for international steam coal is $82/ton. Let’s assume CEIX receives 88% of that price on 16 million tons. This implies an average long-term price of $63/ton. To back into 2024 pricing I assume the average of 2023 ($79/ton) and the long-term price ($63/ton), and 2025 and beyond use $63/ton. Sense-checking this price, $63/ton is the marginal cost of production to produce approximately 825 million tonnes, which is a price that would imply the export market contracts by ~120 million tonnes, or 13%. Depending on whose forecast you use, seaborne demand is expected to grow or only slightly contract over the long-term, so this price is well-supported by the supply/demand balance and production curve.

This methodology implies an enterprise value of $4.5B vs. a current EV of $2.1B. The company is debt-free so that implies a double for the shares. My DCF suggests there is significant upside in the shares if coal prices revert to historical averages from their highs and CEIX is able to capture an increasing share of the export market.

For those unwilling to look that far into the future, the short-run is instructive. The company has committed to return 75% of FCF and has recently announced a preference for share repurchases over dividends. Using the same assumptions above, through 2024 I estimate that the company could repurchase ~34% of its shares outstanding. Assuming no change in the P/E multiple, this represents a 50% return.

In a blue-sky scenario, if the business is stable, the company could repurchase a significantly higher amount of its shares. Mohnish Pabrai has talked about this at length, and shows that with no change in the P/E multiple, an 80% reduction in the share count results in a 5x return, something that is possible if the coal market develops according to my model

The downside case in the shares is that the company does not receive pricing in excess of its costs of production. This is mitigated by the company’s first quartile position on the cost curve. Their balance sheet gives them staying power to withstand any prolonged downdraft in pricing. Anyone who has invested in commodities knows that the downside can be frightening, so I will not attempt to model it, but it’s worth keeping in mind before making an investment. Basically, I’ll be wrong if demand for coal does not stabilize/grow and/or there is a massive oversupply in coal production, which would weigh on pricing.

Catalyst

- Sustained operational performance by the company

- Sustained coal demand and pricing

- Share repurchases

item.title: 2023: The Year of the Lion(sgate)
item.description: ![[2023-the-year-of-the-lionsgate-01.png]] Lions Gate Entertainment Corp. ($LGF-B) at $5.43 is an asymmetric long opportunity representing multi-bagger upside and limited downside over a 12-18…
item.content:encoded:
Lions Gate Entertainment Corp. ($LGF-B) at $5.43 is an asymmetric long opportunity representing multi-bagger upside and limited downside over a 12-18 month time horizon. The stock has been left for dead after management failed to deliver on their promise to secure an investment in the company. Lions Gate is cheap on a sum-of-the-parts basis, which I believe to be well-known by the market. The investment opportunity arises from the sentiment surrounding the stock, which I think is perfectly captured by this Don Coxe quote: “The most exciting returns are to be had from an asset class where those who know it best, love it least, because they have been hurt the most.” Anyone familiar with this stock knows that it is a perennial acquisition target and a deal never materializes. Now is the right time to bet on a potential deal in the near future because the stock is pricing in no chance of success on an eventual sale of one or both its business units, despite management’s statements in regulatory filings to the contrary. Insider purchases have been significant, notably in the last two years and especially recently. What is the stock worth if a spin-off occurs in-line with management’s stated timeline of a company separation by September 2023? In a blue sky case I think the shares are worth $40 (>7x). In a downside case I think the shares are worth $12 (>2x). Until the separation occurs, the stock could be dead money and languish alongside the broader indices and media stocks in what is shaping up to be a vicious bear market.

Business Overview

LGF contains two different businesses that will be separated by September of 2023. One is the Studio business, the other, Starz.

The Studio

The crown jewel within the Studio segment is a film and television library with over 17,000 titles. Management has been investing in the library, successfully growing LTM revenues to $747M today from ~$300M in 2017. Library revenue has 50% cash flow margins. Revenue is driven by both price and volume. An example will help illustrate the pricing power in the library. In 2011, Netflix paid $1M/episode for the rights to stream Mad Men. When that contract expired and came up for renewal a decade later, Amazon paid $3M/episode, or 3x. Obviously, not all content increases in value like that, but it’s important to keep in mind that time is on the side of high quality content. LGF retained the rights to nearly all of their content, allowing them to supply product to the highest bidder each time it comes up for renewal.

Volume is driven by new content that is added to the library, either via M&A or organically. The company is no stranger to M&A, having acquired a handful of studios over the years. Organically, new titles are produced in LGF’s motion picture production business, which is another part of the Studio segment. I won’t spend much time going over the motion picture business since I give it no credit in my valuation as its value is tightly wound together with the library. In short, it’s a low-margin, hit-driven business that has been negatively impacted by Covid. Management has done a good job structuring deals to lay-off risk from any single bad production. Lastly, the Studio contains a diversified, scripted TV content business whose revenue is lumpy, but produces $1B in revenue and $100M in segment profit, on average. TV series are sold to paid-TV networks, subscription video on demand (SVOD) and advertising-based video on demand (AVOD) services, and the timing of revenue is dependent on when deals get signed.

Starz

Lions Gate purchased Starz for $4.4B in 2016. The company was historically a linear-first, streaming-second, premium subscription service, but that has changed with streaming now accounting for 71% of Starz subscribers and 62% of its revenues.

What the market misunderstands about Starz is that the losses from the business are a reflection of heavy international investment by the management team. The domestic business is already profitable and has been for some time. On the most recent earnings call, management finally signaled their intent to stem the losses on the international side. Here’s the company:

“We’ve made a strategic decision to exit 7 international territories, 6 markets in Continental Europe as well as Japan. This process has already begun and will be completed by the end of the fiscal year.”

and

“We expect … our total international subscriber base at year end to exceed 7 million. We expect International segment profit will improve significantly on a quarter-over-quarter basis, starting with the current December quarter. We remain committed to reaching break-even in our international business exiting calendar year 2024 or earlier.”

At quarter-end, Starz International had 14.8M subscribers. This number excludes 2.0M Starz Arabia subscribers. Management just guided to >7M international subscribers as a result of the restructuring, or a ~50% cut. This is management waiving the white flag on growing international subscribers at all costs. Management is now serious about profitability over growth.

Okay, so Starz, which has been a perennial money-loser for the company due to international investments, has finally committed to stop burning money internationally. When international operates at break-even, the profitability from the U.S. segment can shine through.

How did we get here?

Back to the combined company and its languishing stock price. LGF.B shares started the year at approximately $16 and have basically been in a downtrend since. During the summer, the shares bounced in anticipation of management delivering on their promise to sign a deal for an investment in the company. In September, When the market rightly concluded that no deal was forthcoming, the shares resumed their downtrend and haven’t stopped. With no near-term catalysts on the horizon, the stock has been subjected to relentless selling pressure, hitting levels last seen during the March 2020 market crash precipitated by the Covid panic. This difficult to value business that just delivered a big disappointment to investors presents an incredible buying opportunity for contrarian-minded, value investors.

Where do we go from here?

In late 2021, the company announced their intentions to spin Starz and retain the Studio as the parent. An investment in one or both of the businesses was expected alongside the separation. The company changed plans on September 28, 2022 when they announced that they now intend to spin the Studio and retain Starz as the parent. The purpose of splitting the companies is to reveal that the sum of the parts is greater than the whole, so the big picture suggests that it doesn’t matter which entity gets spun. Retaining Starz as the parent allows the company to retain its $1B of low-coupon debt at Starz without having to refinance due to a change in control. More on that later.

It is my understanding that Starz and the Studio are going to be separated in a way that is taxable to the corporate parent but tax-free to shareholders. How is that possible? One way that is possible is if LGF orchestrates a Morris Trust or Reverse Morris Trust transaction. These transactions are basically spin-offs with concurrent investments in either the parent (Morris Trust) or SpinCo (Reverse Morris Trust) entity. For these transactions to qualify as tax-free to the corporate parent, the investment by the third party cannot be for control, i.e. the investment has to be for less than 50% of the entity. However, it is my understanding that a third party can make a greater than 50% investment and still make the transaction tax-free to the shareholders. This would allow LGF to concurrently separate the businesses and have one of them immediately acquired. This is pure speculation on my part, but it is supported by the current fact pattern at the company. Why do I say this? Well the transaction has taken longer than expected. The delay is forgivable in the light of the company having to orchestrate not just a spin-off, but a merger at the same time as a spin-off. A company like Lions Gate, that licenses its owned intellectual property, probably has a lot of legal work to do to get everything lined up. And since LGF sells content to Starz, inter-company agreements need to be worked out ahead of both a deal and a separation. Getting all of the pieces to line up just right isn’t easy, especially as the debt markets freeze up and the stock market sells off. If LGF announces a Morris Trust or Reverse Morris Trust transaction sometime before the Form 10 is filed in March, then that right there represents a catalyst that is not being priced in by the market, a free option if you will. Should this free option end up “in the money”, we would get a valuation marker on one or both of the businesses ahead of the spin-off transaction. This would immediately re-rate the shares higher. Like I said, I’m not counting on it, but I don’t think anyone else is either, which adds to the positively-skewed asymmetry in the shares.

The Importance of Competent Insiders

As previously mentioned, LGF is a perennial M&A target, but a deal never materializes for the company. In fact, it was rumored that the company turned down a $40/share offer from Hasbro in 2018. Recall the shares trade with a $5 handle now. Yikes. So why do I think LGF is finally going to be sold?

Part of it has to do with the involvement of Gordon “Gordy” Crawford. Take a moment to read about his background here if you aren’t familiar with him. He’s a legendary media investor with half a century of experience. At Capital Group, his job required him to get to know all of the media executives better than anyone else in the business. It’s no surprise that out of all the people in the world, it was Gordy who was hanging out at Ted Turner’s ranch when Turner Broadcasting agreed to be acquired by Time Warner.

Gordy has been with Lions Gate since he retired from Capital Group in 2013. It’s been almost a decade since he has been on LGF’s board. So why has Gordy been buying shares of LGF in the open market, hand over fist? His official title on the board is co-chair of the strategic advisory committee. Given his Hollywood connections he probably thinks he’s going to be able to help get a deal done for this company. I don’t think someone with an impeccable investment background is interested in throwing away money. I think he knows what we know, which is that the sum of the parts is greater than the whole, and that the market isn’t giving the company any credit for it. He knows that selling the company and/or splitting it up will help unlock value, and he’s in a unique position to create that outcome. Gordy’s $11.6M worth of open market purchases in 2021 and 2022 dwarf all prior year purchases. He would not start buying shares like he has been if he thought the company would remain a value trap forever.

This is backed up by purchases from the other insiders as well. Since the 8-k came out on 9/28 that sent the stock crashing on the news that no deal had been found, insiders purchased $8.5M worth of stock, or 37% of all insider purchases since 2020 by value.

He Who Shall Not Be Named

Okay, let’s name him. Mark Rachesky. Deservedly or undeservedly, he seems to have a reputation for overplaying his hand and holding his positions past their sell-by dates. Rachesky runs MHR, a hedge fund based out of New York. He has been on the board for over a decade. One of the bear cases on the stock is that Rachesky will never sell. Here’s why I think that doesn’t make any sense. Why would Mark agree to separate Starz and the Studio if he had no intention of selling one or both of the businesses? Rachesky is Chairman of the Board, and board approval is required to complete a corporate action such as a spin-off. The company would not issue an 8-k, a regulatory filing with the SEC, saying that it was contemplating a spin-off if it did not have board approval. So Rachesky is okay with the separation transaction, which is something that is a precursor to a sale of one or both of the businesses.

The other thing about MHR is that it does not have as much control as you might think. Rachesky owns a lot of the A shares, or what are known as the voting shares. The market misperceives these shares to have super-voting rights in an M&A transaction. But they don’t. LGF is a Vancouver-based company, and A and B shares have equal voting rates in an M&A transaction. I’d go as far as saying Gordy’s influence, including the Capital Group stake and the Liberty stake, almost entirely offsets MHR’s votes. So if Gordy wants to sell and MHR wants to drag its feet, there’s a chance that Gordy could have his way and MHR couldn’t do anything about it. When it comes time to vote, who is going to “ride with Rachesky”? Not me.

Valuation

Netflix, the media bellwether, has been crushed alongside the broader market sell-off. Traditional media stocks have not fared any better. In my view this leads to the misperception that all M&A deals need to be massively marked down from prior transaction comparable levels. Comcast CEO Brian Roberts made the following point regarding Comcast’s view of Hulu’s value:

While Disney has pointed to the dip in Netflix’s market cap as an indicator for Hulu’s value, Comcast sees the streamer’s valuation tied to whatever Hulu would fetch as part of a competitive auction of the asset.

The stock market is one thing, competitive auctions are another, and although related, they are not the same thing.

Libraries—of which Lions Gate is one of two remaining large, independent libraries alongside Paramount—are arms-dealers that sell content to streaming platforms.

Streaming platform stocks have been punished in 2022, presumably for their large investments and murky economics. This has weighed on all media stocks, including LGF. If you believe that cord-cutting will continue, i.e. we are not going back to cable as the primary form of TV distribution, then you also believe in a world of streaming platforms, and bigger, more-consolidated platforms than those that exist today. My view is that cord-cutting isn’t complete, and won’t be complete until everything is delivered by subscription video on demand (SVOD) or advertising-based video on demand (AVOD). Until we reach stasis in the streamers’ business models–which we are nowhere near, just see how many households still haven’t cut the cord, or how much streamers are still investing in new content, despite the growth rate slowing–then content will hold its value, and potentially increase in value as rights are renegotiated and streamers acquire content. An arms-dealer like Lions Gate is well-positioned to make money in that environment.

Transaction Multiples

Using management’s newly-issued guidance, the Studio business is expected to generate a range of $420-$470M in EBITDA for fiscal year 2024. Based on transaction comparables, the studio is worth 15x at a minimum in a takeover scenario or $6.3-$7.0B. LGF is one of the few remaining studios that could provide a significant presence in Hollywood, particularly at a time when access to high-quality video content is highly valuable. The company’s library, development opportunities, and talent relationships make it a unique and highly valuable asset. Previous examples of studios being sold for similar valuations include Dreamworks, which was acquired by Comcast for 17x EBITDA in 2016 and MGM, which was acquired by Amazon for 20x EBITDA in 2021.

Starz’s earnings power is slightly more complicated, which I will address in a section further below. Even without giving any credit to Starz, transaction multiples at the Studio make this a compelling investment opportunity.

MGM as a like-for-like Comparison

Recently, Amazon acquired MGM for $8.4B. Comparing LGF to MGM, LGF has a better library, Starz is better than MGM’s Epix, and MGM’s TV business doesn’t do ~$1B in revenue like LGF’s. And MGM doesn’t have a motion picture division like LGF does. It’s very hard to make the case that MGM is more valuable than LGF. Pushback I’ve heard is that MGM has the Bond franchise, but the reality is that they don’t control the Bond franchise–the Broccoli family does–nor do they retain all of its economics. It’s only one marker, and it requires a deep-pocketed, willing buyer, but using MGM as a comp, and it’s a pretty good one, LGF is worth at least $8.5B.

Dreamworks

The Dreamworks acquisition provides a telling example of what a studio is worth in a take-private transaction. There are two points worth considering: 1) Comcast acquired Dreamworks in 2016, well-before the recent stock-market mania that peaked at the end of 2021 and 2) the acquisition was >100% of the then-current comparable trading valuations.

Dreamworks was acquired for $41 per share in cash. Look at the ranges above. In some cases, using market-implied valuations, the take-private price of $41/share was >5x what market multiples implied. This example illustrates how poor of a job the market can do in valuing rare assets like studio business, and also shows how it’s important not to get anchored to recent trading prices when valuing these kinds of businesses. The share price may bounce around, and languish at times, but when it comes time to sell, the valuations are high for these kinds of businesses. Using the Dreamworks multiple, the business is worth $12.3B, which is 4.1x LTM Studio revenue of $3B. This represents the blue-sky case and would be an unbelievable outcome.

Hello Sunshine

In 2019, Reese Witherspoon’s scripted content business Hello Sunshine was valued at $900M. Lions Gate’s diversified scripted content business has >30 scripted series that get sold to paid-TV networks, SVOD and now the growing AVOD (Pluto, Tubi, Roku) market. It does between $80-$100M in segment profit, which fluctuates depending on when deals get signed, and should be worth 10x profit or at least as much as Hello Sunshine, or $800M-$1B.

Margin of Safety

The valuation of the entire company today is underpinned just by the library alone. You can get to a $4B valuation easily on $375M of cash flow. This is one of my favorite things about the investment in LGF at today’s prices–you’re covered by a scarce, valuable asset that can be sold once it is separated from Starz in 2023.

What is Starz Worth on a standalone basis?

The company expects Starz FY 2024 EBITDA to be $175-$225M. The important thing here is the timing of international hitting break-even. Management expects this to occur in the final quarter of 2024, so there will be losses–albeit shrinking ones–up to that point. This depresses Starz FY24 EBITDA. On a run-rate basis, I estimate Starz can generate $300M in EBITDA. At 7x EBITDA for Starz, that’s a $2.1B business, which is significantly below the company’s internal estimate for the business of $2.9B. Recall Starz was acquired for $4.4B and in the most recent quarter, management wrote it down by $1.48B. There is a chance I am being too conservative in appraising its value.

What about all that debt at Starz?

Issuing $1B of debt at a 5.5% coupon in 2021 and terming it out to 2029 ended up creating a hidden asset for Starz. The $1B liability is now worth less than what it is marked at on the balance sheet. At ~60 cents on the dollar, Starz can opportunistically repurchase debt at a discount to face between now and 2029 and deleverage the balance sheet. If I were a private equity firm interested in Starz, I would make an equity investment to provide Starz with cash to do exactly that. Starz’s equity value would re-rate awfully quickly.

Potential Momentum at the Studio

The television business has been running on all cylinders at Lions Gate while motion picture revenue has been stagnant due to a lack of franchise hit releases. That is about to change in the calendar year 2023. In the next year we will see releases of some of Lions Gate’s biggest franchises, including John Wick, The Hunger Games, and Saw.

Buzz from a successful roll-out should support short-term momentum and sentiment in the stock. It’s possible that management is going to use this boost in sentiment to sail off the sunset and sell the Studio business to the highest bidder, but that is pure speculation on my part.

Aside from short-term buzz and a boost to the stock price, the film slate that Lions Gate is releasing has significant cash flow potential, not just from the films themselves, but from the revenue boost they will receive from all prior films in the same franchise. Here’s the company at a recent investor presentation:

“When we released John Wick 3, the revenue ultimates on John Wick 1 and 2 increased by … a couple hundred million dollars of additional revenue. We won’t keep it all, partners, talent participate. When you take that and you understand that. And what that can mean at a company of Lions gates scale and size. Look forward at Wick, Saw, Hunger Games, and on and on … and the rest of business hitting on all cylinders. Think we’re set up in a really strong way to benefit from coming out of this pandemic.”

John Wick 1 and 2 did $200M at the box office, which I will use as a proxy for how big of a hit the film is and its revenue potential. When John Wick 3 was released, it did $327M at the box office. This film was obviously a hit for the company, outdoing the prior two releases. What surprised me was that the action of releasing John Wick 3 added $200M more in revenue to the prior two films. By the way, John Wick 4 is being released in March 2023 with a spin-off film called Ballerina featuring Ana de Armas in the works.

What about the other big franchises? Hunger Games has done $3B at the box office so far over four films. That’s 10x the size of the John Wick franchise, pre John-Wick 3. What could that mean for revenue potential for the prior four Hunger Games films as viewers re-watch that content? Another $2B for the franchise? What about Saw, another film that comes out in 2023 and has done $1B at the box office. I don’t know how to estimate this. But I do know that releasing sequels increases the value of the previously-released films in the same franchise. The market is sleeping on what could be an explosive source of revenue upside for the company once these films hit the screens.

Why is the share price so low?

Management failed to get an investment in either of its businesses and took too long to separate them. I think the market lost a lot of faith in management, which has contributed to the low stock price. There are a few things that argue in management’s favor when considering why they have taken so long to announce a deal.

  1. The debt markets froze up, and “deal stocks”–stocks whose next known catalyst was a corporate action like M&A or outside investment–got crushed as event-driven traders moved onto greener pastures.
  2. Transaction complexity has extended the timeline. Management announced the separation transaction will be tax-free to shareholders but potentially taxable to the parent. Needless to say, getting all the ducks in a row on this transaction is not trivial and requires coordination across multiple stakeholders.
  3. Library rights cadence. For the library to have value, the rights have to be sold to someone. The library content is sold for a set duration, and then comes up for renewal. If someone was interested in buying the library to hoard the content for themselves, they might prefer to have some portion of the library unencumbered. It is conceivable that a buyer is waiting for the right time–when key pieces of content come off of contract–to strike.
  4. Management wants to extract maximum value in a sale and is waiting for the right moment to sell. As discussed above, Lions Gate is releasing a slate of hits in 2023. These hits could help management in negotiating the value of an investment in either business or an M&A transaction for the entire company.

Conclusion

The company is cheap on a sum-of-the-parts basis, and a separation transaction will occur next year, allowing the market to better value those parts. Businesses like Lions Gate aren’t always valued well by the market, and sometimes it takes M&A to unlock value for shareholders. The company could be worth up to $12B or $40 in a blue sky scenario. Downside is protected by the library, and various transaction multiples support multi-bagger stock prices at various points between today’s price at $40/share. LGF is a highly asymmetric stock, and I don’t think you need to know exactly at what price it will be taken-private, you just have to know that your downside is protected, and the upcoming separation process is a catalyst toward unlocking value. Heavy insider buying corroborates this view.

I own shares in the company and could sell at any time, with or without warning. This is not investment advice. Please do your own research and consult a professional before investing in the stock market.

item.title: Prior art? What prior art?
item.description: ![[prior-art-what-prior-art-01.png]] The immediate path forward for Liquidia ($LQDA) comes down to what qualifies as prior art. I think Liquidia is exceptionally well-positioned here based on what…
item.content:encoded:
The immediate path forward for Liquidia ($LQDA) comes down to what qualifies as prior art. I think Liquidia is exceptionally well-positioned here based on what we have learned from the PTAB’s Final Written Decision. Remember, I’m an investor, not a lawyer, and it wouldn’t be the first time I’ve gotten something wrong. Do your own work!

Unsatisfied with my prior post “Someone is wrong on the internet”, I decided to dig a little more into the merits of United Therapeutic (UT)’s request for rehearing of the PTAB case. Recall what UT argued in the original PTAB case:

  1. Liquidia fails to show that JESC and JAHA are prior art to the ’793 patent
  2. Liquidia fails to show that the combination of the ‘212 patent, JESC and JAHA teaches or suggests all the limitations of any of the challenged claims.
  3. Liquidia fails to show that a Person of Ordinary Skill in the Art (POSA) would have had a reason to combine the teachings of these references.

(JESC? JAHA? If what you just read doesn’t make sense, please go back to the beginning and read Parts One, Two, and Three).

Also recall what the PTAB decided in their Final Written Decision (FWD): the PTAB found all three claims in Liquidia’s favor: 1) JESC and JAHA are prior art to the ‘793 patent, 2) the combination of ‘212, JESC, and JAHA teaches or suggests all the limitations of any of the challenged claims, and 3) a POSA would have had a reason to combine the teachings of these references.

Because the PTAB ruled in Liquidia’s favor, they found the ‘793 patent invalid. If and when the PTAB’s decision is affirmed on appeal by the US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit (C.A.F.C.), the ‘793 patent will be canceled, Liquidia will receive final FDA approval for and launch Yutrepia.

Prior to being heard by the C.A.F.C., the PTAB will decide whether to rehear the original case. If they don’t rehear the original case, the C.A.F.C. will hear the appeal. Recall, the C.A.F.C. has sided with the PTAB on ~73% of decisions, so what I believe is the most important thing in the event path, as it stands today, is whether or not Liquidia is likely to win at the PTAB.

In UT’s request for rehearing at the PTAB, they only dispute one of the PTAB’s findings in the FWD. They do not contest points 2 and 3 above. They only contest point one, which is whether or not JESC & JAHA are prior art. In a way, this makes our analysis much simpler since we only have to focus on the key question: does the PTAB think JESC and JAHA qualify as prior art?

Here’s what the PTAB said in their FWD regarding the prior art status of the JESC and JAHA references (“the references”):

“But Petitioner does not rely solely on availability in libraries to show the prior-art status of Voswinckel JESC and Voswinckel JAHA. Instead, Petitioner also argues that “Voswinckel JESC is an abstract presented at the European Society of Cardiology (JESC) Congress,” that Voswinckel JAHA “was publicly presented at the 2004 Scientific Sessions of the American Heart Association,” and that both references were cited in other documents dating from before the priority date of the ’793 patent whose public accessibility is not at issue.”

In the above excerpt from the FWD, the PTAB states that Liquidia made three arguments that support the references’ prior-art status: A) JESC was publicly presented at the European Society of Cardiology Congress, B) JAHA was publicly presented at the 2004 Scientific Sessions of the American Heart Association and C) both references were cited in other documents.

Here is what I believe to be the biggest clue in this back and forth between UT and the PTAB. In UT’s request for rehearing, they contest point C: they say that the references are not prior art because the way they were cited in other documents is invalid (and they might be right about this, but it’s irrelevant in my opinion). But they do not contest points A and B! They say nothing about the fact that the references were publicly presented at conferences. Why am I so confident on the importance of this clue? Let’s go back to the PTAB’s FWD:

“As to both Voswinckel JESC and Voswinckel JAHA, Petitioner’s Reply evidence showing citation to the references in other publicly accessible documents [Clay: this is point C above] is merely additional evidence supporting Petitioner’s original theory that a person of ordinary skill in the art could have located the references.”

The PTAB is saying that public accessibility in other documents — the very thing that UT is contesting — is “merely additional evidence” which supports Liquidia’s claim that a POSA could have located the references. Remove the mere additional evidence from the picture (which is UT’s sole basis for the rehearing request) and a POSA still could have located the references. And if a POSA still could have located the references, then the references are prior art. And if the references are prior art, the ‘793 is invalid. This seems cut and dry to me.

The PTAB has been given an opportunity to clarify their thinking on this matter by the PTAB’s Precedential Opinion Panel (POP). The POP read the FWD at UT’s request and noticed that the PTAB’s support of their opinion was light; the PTAB simply stated their view without supporting analysis (see POP decision here). It is my view that the PTAB will come back and clarify their view on this matter, effectively shutting the door in UT’s face with regards to the rehearing request.

Agree? Disagree? Please let me know in the comments. And don’t be shy about sharing with your Patent Lawyer friends. The more eyes on this, the better!

Side note 1: a reasonable question might be: to what end is UT pursuing this legal strategy? My view is that this legal strategy is consistent with drawing out the clock as long as possible to keep Liquidia’s Yutrepia out of the marketplace. My suspicion is corroborated by UT running that playbook — with the same lawyer from the same law firm — in their attempt to squash competitor SteadyMed. In the case of SteadyMed, UT took them to court for as long as possible. Once it was clear that UT would lose, they decided to acquire SteadyMed.

Side note 2 : @TheIPHawk on Twitter thinks the POP helped Liquidia because once the PTAB concretely lays out their reasoning on the prior art issue, it is less likely to be questioned by the C.A.F.C. during the appeal. His view is that we will get a rehearing decision by the PTAB between 3-6 weeks from 10/27/2022.

item.title: Someone is wrong on the internet!
item.description: This is Part 3 of a series. See [[Liquidia Gold|Part 1 here]] and [[Liquidia Follow-up Part 2|Part 2 here]]. Share enough thoughts publicly on the internet and you’re bound to get something wrong.…
item.content:encoded:
This is Part 3 of a series. See Part 1 here and Part 2 here.

Share enough thoughts publicly on the internet and you’re bound to get something wrong. Like Aladdin who rubs a lamp to magically materialize a genie, a wrong idea on the internet magically materializes an expert in the comments section who is a little too keen to point out your mistakes.

Why does it take someone being wrong on the internet to coax this kind of person out of their lair and into the conversation? I know one thing from experience, and it motivates me to write this blog. It feels psychologically safer to correct someone when they are wrong than it does to expose yourself to humiliation by expressing an original thought. This XKCD comic captures this phenomenon perfectly.

With that in mind, I’m going to expose myself to humiliation, comments section be damned.

This week, Liquidia ($LQDA) received a favorable decision from the Precedential Opinion Panel (POP) of the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) (which Liquidia press-released here. At the time I hit publish on this post, United Therapeutics has made no statement on the matter, which should give some indication as to who benefits from the POP’s decision).

The POP’s mission is to decide issues of exceptional importance to the PTAB. United Therapeutics ($UTHR) made the argument that the PTAB erred in their Final Written Decision (FWD) on the 793 Patent (the last patent preventing Liquidia from launching their flagship drug. See my original post for more context). The POP refused to hear UTHR’s case. Instead, the POP instructed the PTAB judges that issued the FWD to (1) clarify one issue and (2) make a rehearing decision on the original case. It is point number one that I would like to address in this post.

Recall the PTAB’s FWD invalidated the 793 patent on the basis of three pieces of prior art: a separate patent and two publicly-available research publications. The separate patent is not at issue here. Regarding the two research publications, Liquidia made three arguments that demonstrate why they qualify as prior art: (1) the publications were presented at major medical conferences, (2) the publications were publicly accessible at public libraries, and (3) the publications were referenced in other articles in large medical journals, which served as research aids.

Armed with the patent and publicly available research publications, a person of ordinary skill in the art (also known as a “POSA” … think a PhD-level chemist) would be able to create the drug formulation that UTHR patented under the 793 patent. And because a POSA could succeed in this manner, the PTAB invalidated the 793 patent. You can’t “invent” (and subsequently patent) something that already exists in the public domain.

Now in order for United Therapeutics to request a rehearing decision, they have to argue that the PTAB got something wrong in the original hearing. Here’s what they came up with. UTHR claims the research publications are not actually prior art because the date they were referenced in large medical journals is too late to qualify. In other words, UTHR contests point (3) above, but concedes points (1) and (2).

And it is on point (3) that the POP has asked for clarification from the PTAB. For the sake of argument, let’s assume the PTAB got it wrong on point (3), and that UTHR is correct, i.e. point (3) does not qualify the relevant publications as prior art. Then what? Here’s why I think Liquidia still comes out ahead.

It is my assertion that points (1) and (2) are sufficient to qualify the publications as prior art, and even if United Therapeutics wins on point (3), it is irrelevant to the outcome. Why? Part of it has to do with common sense. United Therapeutics is claiming the publications weren’t publicly accessible despite them being publicly accessible. UTHR’s argument is nonsensical.

Another reason why I think Liquidia will prevail has to do with evidentiary standards. In the proceeding with the PTAB, Liquidia has to prevail by a preponderance of the evidence. This means that >50% of the evidence has to weigh in favor of Liquidia. Of the three points in question, by default Liquidia will prevail on 67% of them (two out of three) since only one of the points is contested by UTHR. Is this sufficient to qualify as a preponderance of the evidence? From a legal standpoint, I don’t know. But from a common sense standpoint, two out of three ain’t bad.

In conclusion, I think Liquidia is still highly likely to prevail on the 793 patent. Here’s what Roger Jeffs, CEO Liquidia had to say in response to the POP’s decision:

“Yesterday’s decision clears the way for the PTAB to make a final decision with respect to UTC’s rehearing request. We believe that the requested clarification of the PTAB’s original decision will help to make the PTAB’s decision even stronger. We remain confident that the rehearing request will be denied and that the PTAB’s favorable decision will be affirmed on appeal, thereby unlocking the path to potential approval of YUTREPIA by mid-2024, if not earlier.”

If you think I have this wrong (or right!), make like a genie and find your way to the comments section.

This is Part 2 of a series. See Part 1 here and Part 3 here.

If you’re of a certain age and grew up in America then you’ll recognize this photo.

It’s a photo of the superhero duo Batman and Robin. Batman controls the motorcycle as his sidekick, Robin, sits in the sidecar. Batman is a near-indestructible superhero. Robin is … actually, I don’t remember what he’s good at. And that’s the point. As long as Robin has Batman, and Batman has the wheel, then Robin can sit in the sidecar, confident that Batman won’t lead him astray.

A common mistake I see among investors is that they think they have to know it all. In my experience, sometimes you want to delegate certain aspects of the investment process to individuals with extraordinary skills. This theme recently came to light on social media when Elon Musk’s text messages were revealed in discovery relating to his proposed acquisition of Twitter. Some in the media, who likely don’t understand what it means to take risk, thought the text messages revealed a group of investors who were not so smart because they were investing in Elon Musk, no questions asked. This post does a good job explaining how the media got it precisely backwards. As an investor, you don’t have to know how Elon is going to pull it off. You can look at his track record of success, and correctly identify an individual who has exceptional problem-solving skills and the fortitude to overcome any obstacle in his path. From there, you can decide if it’s a good bet to give him money. Historically, it’s been a great bet.

Sidecar Partners (@SidecarCap) refers to betting on extradorinary people as “sidecar investing” and he lays out his thoughts in this excellent twitter thread. Through Sidecar Partners I learned of Richard Zeckhauser, a professor at the Harvard Kennedy School, who calls sidecar investing “free riding on the superior capability of others” and I can think of no better way of explaining it. If this topic interests you, do yourself a favor and read Zeckhauser’s 36-page paper Investing in the Unknown and Unknowable. It opened my eyes to a new way of thinking, and I hope it does the same for you.

If you’re still with me, I’m going to tie this back to Liquidia and explain why investing alongside CEO Roger Jeffs is a compelling sidecar investment . Here’s what I wrote about Jeffs in my initial post:

Martine Rothblatt, motivated by her daughter’s PAH diagnosis, founded United Therapeutics in 1996. Rothblatt, a lawyer by training and founder of SiriusXM radio, brought on Roger Jeffs, a Ph.D. in pharmacology, in 1998 as Director of Research, Development and Medical of UTHR. Together, Rothblatt and Jeffs grew United Therapeutics into a PAH powerhouse by their decision to commercialize treprostinil in 2002. Today, treprostinil is sold under the brand names Remodulin for infusion, Orenitram for oral, and Tyvaso for inhalation. All three brand names are owned by United Therapeutics.

After an 18 year career, Jeffs retired from UTHR as co-CEO (a title he shared with Rothblatt) and President. In January of 2022, Jeffs became CEO of Liquidia. Jeffs owns 2.7% of Liquidia’s shares outstanding, approximately $10M worth.

To lay it out more explicitly, Jeffs’ scientific know-how enabled United Therapeutics to start from nothing and grow into the pulmonary arterial hypertension powerhouse that it is today. Before Rothblatt and Jeffs entered the scene, there wasn’t even a company working on the problem. If anyone knows this industry, it’s Roger Jeffs.

After retiring as co-CEO of United Therapeutics, Jeffs became a director of RareGen, a company focused on rare disease pharmaceutical products that acquired the right to promote Sandoz’s first-to-file generic of Remodulin (treprostinil) for the treatment of patients with PAH. Liquidia bought RareGen in 2020 and brought Jeffs along as a board member. In January of 2022, Jeffs was appointed CEO of Liquidia. Would someone with his knowledge of PAH take this position if he didn’t see potential for the company? Here’s what I think. He would not take the position if he thought the technology was a flop. This is what I mean by outsourcing my technical due diligence to Jeffs. It doesn’t mean the company is going to be a success, or that the stock will work. It simply means that there is significant enough potential in the technology for an expert in the field to take a large bet on it. Of course, I’ll continue my due diligence to identify any potential red flags with the technology. For example, I’ve already identified another expert that I would like to speak with on the topic (whether they want to speak with me is another question altogether). If I’m successful on that front, I’ll write it up for you.

As a reminder, Jeffs is heavily invested in the success of Liquidia to the tune of $10M. He has been buying in the open market. Most recently, he purchased ~$250K worth of shares at $5.57, above today’s price of ~$5.20. Below is a snapshot of his open market purchases this year, which occurred in the middle of the ongoing litigation between Liquidia and United Therapeutics.

Thanks for reading and I hope to have more updates in the near-future.

item.content:encoded:
This is Part 1 of a series. See Part 2 here and Part 3 here.

The following is a very high risk stock. Please do your own due diligence and do not rely on this article for your research. I’m an investor and I get things wrong all the time.

Okay, this post is about Liquidia Corp.

Overview

Liquidia Corp ($LQDA) is a $340M market cap, $261M enterprise value biotech company that manufactures drugs using their proprietary particle engineering system. They intend to commercialize their flagship product, Yutrepia, for the treatment of the orphan disease pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), a $5B market in the United States. PAH is a fatal disease characterized by increased pressure in the pulmonary vasculature and that often results in heart failure.

Unlike many publicly traded biotech companies, Liquidia faces zero clinical trial risk. Yutrepia is tentatively approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), which means that the drug is almost ready to launch. To receive final approval from the FDA and launch the drug, Liquidia needs to successfully resolve the outstanding patent infringement claims levied against them by United Therapeutics ($UTHR), the leader in the PAH space.

Despite recent material wins on the patent litigation front, the share price of Liquidia implies a low probability of their legal success. With shares trading at $5.42 I estimate the market is implying a 36% chance that Liquidia prevails; I think the odds are much closer to 75% which justify a $13.70 share price today (+153%). If Liquidia is successful and launches Yutrepia then the shares are worth ~$18 (+232%) at launch. If Liquidia is unsuccessful, the shares are likely to collapse, probably to the vicinity of $1 (-82%). I repeat, this is a high risk stock.

Brief Company Backgrounds

Liquidia’s biggest competitor is the market leader, United Therapeutics (UTHR), whose flagship product, Tyvaso, delivers patients treprostinil through a nebulizer. UTHR’s market cap is $10B and the company generates revenue of $1.8B per year, 43% from the sale of inhaled treprostinil and 90% from the sale of PAH treatments more broadly (UTHR sells infused, oral and inhaled PAH medicines).

Martine Rothblatt, motivated by her daughter’s PAH diagnosis, founded United Therapeutics in 1996. Rothblatt, a lawyer by training and founder of SiriusXM radio, brought on Roger Jeffs, a Ph.D. in pharmacology, in 1998 as Director of Research, Development and Medical of UTHR. Together, Rothblatt and Jeffs grew United Therapeutics into a PAH powerhouse by their decision to commercialize treprostinil in 2002. Today, treprostinil is sold under the brand names Remodulin for infusion, Orenitram for oral, and Tyvaso for inhalation. All three brand names are owned by United Therapeutics.

After an 18 year career, Jeffs retired from UTHR as co-CEO (a title he shared with Rothblatt) and President. In January of 2022, Jeffs became CEO of Liquidia. Jeffs owns 2.7% of Liquidia’s shares outstanding, approximately $10M worth.

The Patent Infringement Cases

United Therapeutics sued Liquidia for infringement of three of their patents: U.S. Patent Numbers 9,604,901 (the 901 patent), 9,593,066 (066), and 10,716,793 (793). By suing Liquidia for patent infringement UTHR guaranteed that, even if they lose in court, Yutrepia’s launch would be delayed by several years due to the time it takes to try and appeal the various court decisions.

Before the lawsuit, Liquidia was a promising drug company targeting an established, multi-billion dollar market with a superior drug-delivery mechanism. Today, Liquidia’s stock is a bet on the outcome of patent litigation. Similar to when an investment grade bond is downgraded and holders have to automatically sell, this lawsuit triggered indiscriminate selling amongst LQDA holders and the share price has languished ever since. This lawsuit is why the opportunity exists.

Liquidia can launch Yutrepia if all asserted patent claims are found to be either invalid or not infringed. So far, Liquidia has definitively won on two out of the three patents (901 and 066), and has scored a major victory on the third patent (793).

Definitive Victories

The 901 patent is a product by process patent for the preparation of treprostinil, the ingredient in UTHR’s Remodulin. In June 2021, during a claim construction hearing for Hatch-Waxman litigation, UTHR agreed to the entry of judgment of Liqudia’s non-infringement of the 901 patent. The 901 patent is no longer a roadblock for Liquidia – they won.

The 066 patent is a product by process patent for the preparation of treprostinil, the active ingredient in Remodulin, relating to UTHR’s product Tyvaso, a nebulized solution for the treatment of PAH. In August 2022, the same court in the Hatch-Waxman litigation mentioned above found that all 066 patent claims asserted have been found to be either invalid or not infringed. Liquidia won on the 066 patent.

Victory in the Making?

Two down, one to go. Liquidia has one more hurdle to clear: the 793 patent which covers treprostinil administration by inhalation. This patent was issued by the US Patent and Trademark Office (PTO) in the month following UTHR’s filing of the lawsuit. Despite the delayed timing, UTHR was able to add the 793 patent to the proceedings and make it a gating factor for Liquidia.

The 793 patent is also where the story becomes slightly more confusing. Liquidia made two separate cases for the invalidity of the 793 patent: one in front of the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) of the PTO in an Inter Partes Review (IPR) and one in front of the district court as part of the Hatch-Waxman litigation.

Liquidia was successful in invalidating the 793 patent in front of the PTAB at the IPR. This is a hugely important point. While not sufficient to end the patent issue today, it is a necessary step on the way to victory. Let’s leave the IPR hearing and go back to the Hatch-Waxman litigation for a second.

Unfortunately for Liquidia, they were not successful in front of the district court in the Hatch-Waxman (HW) litigation for the 793 patent. Why? Because Liquidia was estopped, or precluded from making the same argument in both the HW and IPR proceedings. Liquidia decided to use their strongest case in the IPR and won. By default, the HW case was decidedly weaker and Liquidia lost.

What does it all mean, and how does Liquidia move forward from here? The most straightforward way for Liquidia to prevail on the 793 patent is to have the PTAB’s IPR decision affirmed on appeal. This process takes time and will likely conclude sometime in 2023/2024 (more on the timeline later). Once this occurs, the 793 patent will be thrown out, the district court’s ruling will be irrelevant, and Liquidia will launch Yutrepia.

A second avenue for Liquidia to get to market is to launch Yutrepia “at-risk.” Today, they are precluded from doing that due to the HW ruling. However, Liquidia has asked the judge who ruled in HW to effectively look at the big picture. Liquidia’s rationale, among other things, is that they have already invalidated the 793 patent – the only patent stopping them from launch – in the PTAB and are just waiting on the decision to be affirmed on appeal which happens 73% of the time. Liquidia thinks they should be able to launch now and face the consequences of the appeal process later. If Liquidia launches now and wins on appeal at a future date, then no harm, no foul. If Liquidia launches now and loses on appeal at a future date, then they owe damages to United Therapeutics. This outcome makes the most sense to me, but I am not a lawyer and don’t want confirmation bias to enter my thought process. To be clear, Liquidia’s lawyers are presenting a far more sophisticated legal argument than what I just described. Because it is a sophisticated legal argument I am not qualified to handicap its chances of success. Accordingly, I consider the prospect of a favorable judgment a “free option” that could payoff as soon as this month.

Timeline

Standing between Liquidia and launch are the following steps: The PTAB rehearing request being denied, an appeal filed, record transmittal, briefing, oral arguments, and a decision. To bracket the timeline I think the shortest case is an August 2023 launch and the longest case is in-line with Liquidia’s guidance of a mid-2024 launch. The key variables are 1) how fast the rehearing request is denied and 2) whether or not Liquidia receives a Rule 36 decision. On point 1, the PTAB aims to decide on rehearing cases within a month of receiving a request. UTHR waited until the very last day – consistent with running out the clock on a weak case – in mid-August. One month from that date has already past, but it’s possible that the rehearing request is denied this month, October 2022. The worst case I have seen is a 9 month lag between a rehearing request and a decision from the PTAB – this puts approximately 7 months between best/worst case on the PTAB decision. On point 2, if Liquidia receives a Rule 36 decision, that shaves 3 months off the decision timeline. Otherwise, a Full Written Decision would take 3 months. Altogether, best case is August 2023 and worst case is June 2024. Liquidia guided the market to “mid-2024 or earlier” which is conservative and the best decision; better to underpromise and overdeliver.

Why I think Liquidia Receives a Rule 36 Decision

Federal Circuit Rule 36 specifies that “the court may enter a judgment of affirmance without opinion” when certain specified conditions exist. A Rule 36 Decision “does not endorse or reject any specific part of the trial court’s reasoning” and is non-precedential, i.e. not binding on the court. These judgments are usually handed down after the court hears oral arguments. What does this mean? It means the timeline to affirm the PTAB’s decision on appeal can be dramatically shortened by a Rule 36 Decision. I think Liquidia is likely to receive one due to the precendent set by United Therapeutics in their eerily similar case vs. SteadyMed. SteadyMed filed an IPR for one of UTHR’s patents which also happened to be a process to prepare treprostinil, the active ingredient in Remodulin. Long story short, the patent was found to be invalid by the PTAB, and received a Rule 36 Decision when it was affirmed on appeal. Liquidia’s case is so close to SteadyMed’s that one might think UTHR is running the same exact legal playbook to run out the clock in the face of an inevitable defeat. Note: when the clock ran out, UTHR ultimately acquired SteadyMed.

What’s it Worth?

What’s it worth? I will better flesh out the math in a future post. Let’s assume LQDA is able to capture 8% of the PAH market (PAH WHO Groups 1 and 3) by 2028. In that scenario, I estimate the company is able to generate $1B in revenue. At a peer multiple of 3.2x EV/Sales, discounted back to today at 10%, I arrive at a share price of $34. This seems like a reasonable bull case and assumes a lot of execution success.

If you’d rather run napkin math, consider the following. UTHR is worth about $10B. What’s a post-clinical, imminently-commercial competitor worth, arguably one with a better product and led by a pioneer of the industry? I’d say 10% of UTHR is fair. That gets you to ~$1B or $18/sh.

Today the market implies Liquidia has a 36% chance of prevailing in court. I think the odds are much closer to 75% which justify a $13.70 share price today (+153%). If Liquidia is successful and can launch Yutrepia then I think the shares will re-price to $18 (+232%) in short order. Longer term, Liquidia has the potential to materially penetrate the PAH market and be worth in excess of $30. If Liquidia is unsuccessful, the shares are likely to collapse to the vicinity of $1 (-82%).

Risks

Liquidia is facing a formidable challenger. Martine Rothblatt’s identity is tied up with the success of United Therapeutics. By all accounts, Rothblatt does not like to lose. Expect UTHR to fight Liquida tooth-and-nail here. As mentioned several times already, the downside to the stock is substantial (-82%) if Liquidia loses in court.

A Note on Insider Ownership

The Hatch-Waxman decision was handed down at the end of August and insiders started buying almost immediately. Insiders had already been buying ahead of the HW decision. CEO Roger Jeffs owns ~$10M of stock. Fund Management Company and Board Member Caligan Partners owns ~25% of the company! Yes, they bought after the HW concluded, despite Liquidia’s loss on the 793 patent.

item.content:encoded:
In poker, a freeroll is a tournament with no entry free. By participating, your financial downside is zero, and the only downside is the opportunity cost of your time. Your upside is determined by how well you play (and some luck). It is the distribution of potential outcomes that makes a freeroll such a compelling investment idea, and it’s no surprise they rank amongst my favorites. Heads, I win. Tails, I don’t lose (too much).

Shell Midstream (ticker: ) is an equity that I think represents a freeroll at today’s price. Full disclosure: SHLX closed at $14.07 today; my cost basis is in the $13s.

What makes this a freeroll? SHLX is undergoing a transaction whereby its parent, Shell plc (ticker: ) has offered to acquire the SHLX units it currently does not own (SHEL currently owns ~70% of SHLX) at $12.89/unit. Math majors will notice that $12.89 represents 8% downside to today’s closing price; not exactly a freeroll. The math is correct, but assuming the deal closes (more on this later), consider the following: between now and the anticipated close, an investor today receives one $0.30 distribution per SHLX unit. That reduces your cost basis to $14.07 - $0.30 or $13.77. Your downside to the deal price is now 6.4%. Still not free, but it’s looking better. How do we improve upon this? This is where deal mechanics and precedent transactions play a key role.

Because SHLX is structured as an MLP, the take-private offer from SHEL isn’t what you would typically see in a situation involving a publicly traded company, or C-Corp. With a C-Corp, any acquirer would offer a premium price to get shareholders and the board of directors to agree to the acquisition. This is not required in an MLP takeover transaction; the general partner (in this case, SHEL), can legally acquire its subsidiary MLP at any price of its choosing. And you will notice that the offer price of $12.89/unit was done at a 0% premium to SHLX’s last closing price before the deal was announced.

It is my contention that the initial, 0% premium offer by SHEL is simply an opening move. A deal tactic. Why do I think this? Because now that the offer has been announced, a special committee of outsiders has been appointed by SHEL to evaluate the deal. Their job is to negotiate on behalf of the minority (non-SHEL) unitholders. Yes, they were appointed by SHEL and could simply do SHEL’s bidding. I am not that cynical. I think the special committee members work for themselves and care about their reputations. Ultimately, they do not wish to be sued for harming minority unitholders, who in this case are primarily retail investors (MLPs are marketed to yield-seeking retail investors). My base case is that the special committee will evaluate the deal and come up with a fair price for both SHEL and SHLX.

Precedent transactions are on my side. Historically, when an MLP take-private transaction of this kind is announced, the initial offer is raised by at least 15%. A 15% increase to the initial offer would result in 7.5% upside from today’s close if you include the upcoming $0.30 distribution slated to be paid in early August. A 15% increase represents my base case.

There is also potential for a much higher deal price. SHEL’s offer was announced in February of this year. At the time of the announcement, the oil price was lower and the outlook for oil and gas had not reached the fever pitch that we see today. Further, oil majors like SHEL invest on multi-decade time horizons. SHEL’s acquisition comes at a time when certain refined product and offshore pipelines are under-earning. Giving SHLX full credit for its under-earning assets could see a deal price of $20/unit. Recall, SHLX went public at $23/unit in 2014 when oil prices were ~$80/bbl vs. ~$100/bbl today. A revised price to $20/unit plus the $0.30 distribution equates to 44% upside.

One final point. My analysis hinges on the deal closing. I think it’s almost a certain thing—there are no guarantees in investing!—that the deal closes. Why? Because SHLX is just a tax structure. SHEL already owns and operates these assets. The acquisition is simply the undoing of a complicated financial transaction that was done for tax purposes. The tax benefits no longer exist, and it makes sense for SHEL to bring the ~30% of SHLX it does not own back under the SHEL umbrella. There are no regulatory reviews, no financing risk, no shareholder votes, etc. If SHEL wants to close the deal, they will, and I can’t think of anything that would stop them at this point.

In summary, the only way I see this investment losing money is if SHEL does not raise their initial offer by more than 6.8%. I think the odds of this happening are less than 5%. As for the shape of the remaining distribution: it’s unknowable. Precedent transactions suggest initial offers are raised by at least 15%, and in some cases, >100% (see Hoegh LNG). Heads, I win. Tails, I don’t lose (too much!).

item.title: What’s the right multiple for the largest zero-carbon energy producer in the United States?

item.content:encoded:
What’s the right multiple for the largest zero-carbon energy producer in the United States? In this writeup I hope to show you that Exelon is a classic Michael Price “Steak and Sizzle” investment which offers downside protection and a free option on ESG-driven upside. EXC is trading at $56/sh and in my base case is worth $68/sh (+21%). In an upside case EXC could be worth $100/sh in value (+79%).

Today, Exelon houses two different business lines: 1) regulated utilities and 2) electric power generation & retailing. On February 1, 2022, Exelon will effect a tax-free spin to separate the two companies into Exelon “RemainCo” (utilities) and Constellation “CEG” (generation & retailing). The two businesses have different earnings streams which attract different investor bases. Utility investors award high PE multiples to stable, predictable earnings and that is what RemainCo will offer. ESG investors love zero-carbon emissions, and CEG has the makings of an ESG powerhouse.

RemainCo Overview

RemainCo’s regulated utility business is the largest transmission and distribution-only utility in the United States with a $48B rate base. Areas of operation include Illinois (29% of rate base), MD (21%), PA (17%), DC (5%), NJ (4%), and DE (3%). The balance of the rate base is FERC Transmission (21%).

RemainCo’s regulated utilities are granted franchised monopolies. This protects them from competition, but in exchange RemainCo’s earnings power is capped by regulators. As a result, the earnings stream is generally predictable and is awarded high multiples from defensive investors. RemainCo guides to $2.25 of 2022 EPS which is expected to grow ~7% for the next three years. Utility peers whose EPS exhibit low volatility and grow in the mid-single digits include CMS, DTE, WEC, ES, LNT, ED and SO. These peers trade at 22x 2022 operating EPS. Applying a peer multiple of 22x to RemainCo’s 2022 guidance results in $50/sh for this business.

Constellation Overview

Hidden inside Exelon is the largest producer of zero-carbon electricity in the United States. CEG produces 65% more zero-carbon electricity than the next largest producer (NextEra) and >600% more than the median power producer. As a result, one of of every nine MWhs of clean electricity produced in the United States is by CEG.

Further, its carbon footprint is unmatched: across its entire fleet, for each MWh produced, CEG generates 98lbs of CO2. This is 78% less than its next closest peer, PSEG, and 91% less than the median investor-owned power producer. (Source: M.J. Bradley & Associates Benchmarking Air Emissions, July 2021 https://www.mjbradley.com/sites/default/files/Presentation_of_Results_2021.pdf)

How do they do it? Nuclear. CEG’s combined fleet provides nearly 90% carbon-free electricity to a customer base including utilities, municipalities, cooperatives, commercial & industrial entities, residences, and public sector entities. States such as Illinois have recognized the need for nuclear to meet long-term, state-sponsored zero-carbon emission goals. To illustrate this point, CEG was going to de-commision two nuclear power plants in Illinois in 2021. The state decided that was untenable, and granted CEG incentives which amounts to ~$150m/year. Accordingly, CEG reversed their decision to retire the plants.

RemainCo’s valuation above implies that CEG is trading at $7/sh of value or 3.2x EV/EBITDA. Note, some sell-side estimates have missed the following point. CEG today has $4.6b in total debt. However, immediately before the spin, CEG will receive a cash payment from Exelon of $1.75b. This cash payment will bring the net debt balance at CEG to $1.2bn. Using RemainCo’s valuation above, and the correct balance sheet as outlined in the Form 10, I estimate that CEG’s implied valuation is $7/sh or 3.2x EV/EBITDA.

Power generators have less predictable earning streams than regulated utilities. Accordingly, power generators such as NRG and Vistra trade at 7.0-8.5x 2022 EV/EBITDA. Applying that multiple to CEG results in $18/sh of value in my base case.

Things get interesting if CEG becomes an ESG darling. Predominately renewable power producers trade on very high EV/EBITDA multiples. For example, Brookfield Renewable Partners trades at 24x 2022 EV/EBITDA, and NextEra Energy, the next largest clean energy producer after CEG, trades at 17x. Taking the midpoint and applying a 20x multiple results in $50/sh in an upside case.

In conclusion, EXC’s undemanding valuation protects you on the downside and offers +21% upside in my base case and effectively a free look at ESG mania which could result in an upside scenario of +79%.

DISCLAIMER: I benefit from this stock’s appreciation, and have acquired it at a price below the current one. I do not have a specific exit price in mind at this point, and make no promises that I will notify anyone when I sell. I therefore prescribe two grains of salt and a ton of due diligence.

I do not hold a position with the issuer such as employment, directorship, or consultancy.
I and/or others I advise hold a material investment in the issuer’s securities.
